articles.title: Purple's DreamLayer pillow is total luxury for all sleep styles — but there's one big reason I can't give it 5 stars
articles.content: Purple DreamLayer Pillow: Review in brief Online sleep brand Purple has made some of the best pillows we've tested, earning praise like " ultimate relaxation " from our expert testing team. With that ringing in my ear, I jumped at the chance to test the Purple DreamLayer pillow, a multi-layer design that's made to match every sleep style. Purple DreamLayer Pillow At A Glance Type: Memory foam, GelFlex Grid Best for: All sleep positions, hot sleepers Sizes: 22.25" x 16.125", 31.75" x 16.125" Trial: 30 nights Warranty: 1-year Price: From $229 at Purple Purple's iconic GelFlex Grid is a mainstay of its mattresses (we rate many Purple beds among the best mattresses you can buy online). In the DreamLayer pillow a micro-version of this same grid is used to provide pressure relief . Think of it like a cloud is cuddling your head. Removable 'booster' layers give the DreamLayer pillow three potential pillow lofts , or heights. Picking the right loft for your sleep style helps prevent neck strain and with the DreamLayer, you can play about with what works for you. As a stomach sleeper, I swiftly ditched the booster. But side sleepers should appreciate the chance to tweak. Boosters also add support to the pillow, so side sleepers won't feel like they're sinking all the way through. It's a strong all-rounder and while I can't guarantee it'll suit every sleep style, it does a good job at appealing to most. Especially with the breathable feel, which prevents overheating and limits night sweats . (Image credit: Future) The big drawback is the price. The MSRP starts at $229 which puts it at the top end of the premium bracket. But after sleeping on it for over three weeks, I don't think that should turn you away. Here's why... Purple DreamLayer Pillow: Price & deals I’m a big believer in investing in sleep comfort. But even I'll admit $229 is a steep price to pay for a pillow. And that’s just for a standard size — you’ll pay $269 for a king. Purple mattress sales do happen semi-regularly, although they’re notoriously hard to predict. However, patience can bring you a saving. You’re most likely to get money off when you buy two or more pillows, but sometimes Purple does offer discounts on single pillows. To put the price into context, the top-rated Coop Sleep Goods Original has an MSRP of $89, while the luxury Saatva Latex Pillow has an MSRP of $165. However, $200+ isn't a shocking price for a luxury or organic pillow. The Downright Mackenza White Down pillow, for example, is $212 for a firm feel. And Norvegr's heritage luxury pillows start at $635 in a standard size (but they will refresh your pillow every five years.) Purple's benefits are a little limited, with a 30-night sleep trial and a 1-year warranty. In comparison, Coop offers a 100-night trial and a 5-year warranty; among the best you can expect for a pillow. DreamLayer pillow (standard): $229 One of Purple's premium grid pillows, the DreamLayer pillow comes in two sizes with prices starting at $229. At the time of writing you can save 10% by doubling up your purchase but we'll be keeping our eye out for a better discount in the Black Friday mattress and sleep sales . View Deal Purple DreamLayer Pillow: Design & materials (Image credit: Future) There are quite a few unusual features to the Purple DreamLayer Pillow. We’ll start at the top, where you find Purple’s GelFlex Grid. This is made from hyper-elastic polymer, molded into a grid shape. It’s designed to deliver comfort that adapts to your every curve and it's found in all Purple mattresses. Next is the MicroAir Foam. This is attached to the GelFlex Grid and uses “billions of microscopic air capsules” to create airflow and contouring. Finally, there are two removable layers. These are made from standard polyurethane foam. Adding and removing layers changes both the pillow loft and who the pillow suits, as so: Loft Best for No booster 5" Back and stomach sleepers 1 booster 6" Side and combination sleepers 2 boosters 7" Side…

articles.title: Google's First Data Center Satellite Is Online and Writing Poetry
articles.content: Google's first experimental space-based data center is operational after launching earlier this month, successfully running its Gemma 4 AI model aboard a satellite and generating a haiku about being in orbit. TechCrunch reports: The satellite, which carries four Google Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and generates up to 1 kW of electricity, is intended to pave the way for future networks of close-flying satellites performing large inference workloads in orbit. However, the power demands of the TPU mean it can only turn one on for about 20 minutes at a time, complicating the already tricky business of space-to-ground communications. After a commissioning process that tested out the satellite's subsystems over about three weeks, the spacecraft was ready to work. When engineers on the ground sent their first prompt this week, they asked the model pre-loaded onto the satellite, Google DeepMind's Gemma 4, to write a haiku about being in space. And thus: Blue marble below Data streams in silent grace Starlight feeds my core. The ongoing test campaign will examine how the chips perform under thermal stress and in the space radiation environment. [...] If the TPUs onboard this spacecraft prove capable, the next step will be launching two more satellites equipped with the advanced chips in 2027. Those spacecraft will support higher power generation and demonstrate inter-satellite optical links. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.author: BeauHD

articles.title: AI vendors are relearning the oldest rule in the data business
articles.content: Long before anyone trained a model on customer data, the marketing data business worked out the terms for pooling it. Catalog retailers in the 1990s joined data cooperatives that combined their transaction histories so each member could find new buyers, and the arrangements held together because the rules were blunt. A retailer contributed data to receive modeled prospects; no member got a rival's customer file; and a company that stopped contributing stopped receiving. Card fraud consortia run on similar give-to-get terms. Nobody would call these systems elegant, but every participant understood the trade. Software vendors building AI features are now running into the same question, usually without the rules. Traditional software sat on top of a customer's data and operated on it. AI products learn from data, and on a multi-tenant platform, that learning rarely stays within a single account. One company's records can sharpen the enrichment, lead scoring, and recommendations delivered to thousands of others. A vendor can improve its product for every customer by relying on the work of a few, and most contracts say nothing about whether that trade is fair. The customer still owns its data in any legal sense. Ownership alone doesn't answer who benefits. Users push back on sharing hard-earned data HubSpot learned how touchy the question has become when it announced plans to pool enrichment data across customer accounts, including business contact details, employer information, and email deliverability signals, to improve prospect records platform-wide. Every account was in by default. Within days, the company dropped the plan and promised that any future enrichment feature built on customer data would be opt-in. HubSpot had stated clearly that core CRM records would never be shared without permission, so privacy in the usual sense wasn't what upset the sales and RevOps teams, who pushed back. Their concern was harder to answer. Years of work spent cleaning and enriching their own contact data were about to improve the prospecting tools available to every other customer, competitors included, and nobody had asked what they would get for it. The product terms that allowed the change had been updated nearly two years before most customers heard about them. AI creates accidental data companies Plenty of software companies adding AI tools have never had to think this way. They are becoming data companies one model at a time, often without deciding to. Whether a customer's information feeds a shared model is often determined by a product team working toward a launch date rather than by anyone who owns the commercial relationship, and the answer is expressed in terms few buyers read. McKinsey's 2026 survey on AI trust found that only about 30% of organizations have reached a mature level in AI strategy, governance, and controls. Pooled training data tends to fall between legal, product, and sales, with no single team feeling responsible for explaining it. The need for strong exit clauses Buyers will force the issue long before regulators do. Security certifications and uptime guarantees became standard contract language over the past decade because enough customers asked for them that vendors stopped arguing, and AI data terms are heading down the same road. Procurement teams are starting to ask whether their data trains or enriches models used by other customers, whether participation is opt-in, and whether it can be switched off later without losing core features. The more demanding buyers want to know what a contributing customer receives that a non-contributor doesn't. Exit terms will be the hardest part to write. A customer can cancel a contract and demand its records back, but data that has already shaped a production model can't be cleanly pulled out again. Retraining is expensive, and removing one customer's influence from a live model remains an unsolved problem for most vendors. A vendor can honestly say it deleted every…

articles.title: 7 ways to use ChatGPT to shop smarter — and the prompts to help you save
articles.content: 2026 has felt like it’s been in fast-forward mode all year long. Once everyone dumps their Halloween costumes and buys all the leftover candy from the local pharmacy on sale, we’ll be carving turkeys and opening Christmas presents before we know it. Speaking of presents, there’s going to be that annual trend of shopping for you and loved ones coming up real soon. And with the advent of AI, a lot of people will be referring to their preferred chatbots to help them make smart shopping decisions. I’ve gotten accustomed to asking ChatGPT to help me do just that by highlighting the finest products, checking if the deals attached to them are actually good or not, comparing two products I’m deciding between and more. For the folks reading this right now who regularly find themselves with a credit card in one hand and the other on your keyboard, allow me to send forth these tips that’ll help you shop smarter. By working with ChatGPT to do some proper research with the following prompts in tow, you’ll quickly realize just how helpful OpenAI’s chatbot can be when the time arrives to make another online purchase. 1. Find the best product that fits within your budget (Image credit: Shutterstock) I’m a hardcore gamer, so I’m always in the market for the best headsets, arcade sticks and third-party controllers whenever one of the ones I own stops working. Plus, I’m usually on the lookout for additional bookcases and video game storage stand towers. ChatGPT comes in handy whenever I get the urge to buy one of those types of products and find the best options while also keeping my budget in mind. For everyone else, this method and the prompt that goes right along with it should help you discover whatever you’re looking for at the most approachable price: I'm looking to buy [product type] for [intended use]. My maximum budget is [$X]. My top three priorities are [priorities]. Recommend five options, explain the pros and cons of each, identify the best value for money, and tell me which features aren't worth paying extra for. Use current sources where possible and link to the evidence. 2. Compare two or more products to see which one is worth getting (Image credit: Shutterstock) Weighing your options before you finally click the “Buy” button is a common practice for many. ChatGPT also plays the part of a great decision-maker as it looks up all the crucial factors that will help sway your final buying decision. The following prompts work exceptionally well when you’re looking to choose between some high-value tech, such as laptops, headphones, TVs or kitchen appliances: Compare [Product A] and [Product B] for my needs: [describe how I'll use them]. Build a side-by-side comparison of performance, durability, ease of use, warranty, running costs and price. Highlight the meaningful differences, flag any trade-offs, and recommend one based on my priorities. Verify specifications against manufacturer sources. 3. Check whether a deal is actually a deal worth spending on (Image credit: Shutterstock) 4. Look up customer reviews for red and green flags (Image credit: Shutterstock) For pieces of hardware, I love to go digging in the customer reviews section to look for the bad ones. Those five-star reviews are fine and all, but I’m more open to checking out those reviews that are 3 stars and lower. The people who hand out those reviews with paragraphs of valid criticisms always make me weigh my options even more when choosing what new piece of tech to add to my room next. ChatGPT can go beyond star ratings and tap into the following prompt to find the most recurring complaints from customers, the failure points that come up the most and issues that pop up the most after weeks or months of use: Research customer feedback for [product]. Find recurring positive and negative themes across independent reviews and customer discussions. Pay particular attention to durability, reliability, misleading product descriptions, customer service and problems that…

articles.title: Forget muddy shoes: 61% of Americans agree this is the single rudest holiday houseguest habit
articles.content: Even though I’m trying hard to ignore the calendar, the holiday season is nearly here. Between stirring up batches of homemade mincemeat (yes, I really do) and preparing a guest list, my mind has turned to the collision of generational habits around the dinner table. While I was taught to politely remove my shoes at the door and never arrive empty-handed — how much does this old–school etiquette stand up today? You might get away with bending the rules around close family, but how should you behave when under the roof of a less familiar host? Luckily, you don’t need to guess the right social etiquette when you’re attending a holiday party, because furniture company Joybird has done the groundwork for you. It surveyed over 2,800 U.S. adults to pinpoint what modern houseguest courtesy looks like, from non-negotiable house rules and off-limits conversations to outdated customs. Here’s a deep dive into what they found. Don’t make this biggest etiquette mistake (Image credit: Getty Images) Forget about not taking your shoes off when you cross the threshold; the rudest etiquette mistake is snooping. It was the most hated behavior across generations, scoring 61% with nothing else coming close. The rudest etiquette mistake is snooping. It was the most hated behavior across generations, scoring 61% with nothing else coming close. As a home writer, it’s tough to stick to; I’m always desperate to peek at everyone’s home decor, but it’s one unwritten houseguest rule you shouldn’t break. So next time you’re a guest, don’t snoop in private rooms. And don’t even think about peering into closets, drawers, and cabinets — they’re all strictly off-limits. What other bad habits cross the line (Image credit: Shutterstock) Although snooping was undoubtedly the rudest behavior that the generations agreed upon, turning up sick came second. So if you have a slight sniffle or feel a bit queasy, you’re better off staying home. At 42%, it was the second most hated behavior among the three oldest generations, and you can see why. Your slight sniffle could be the gift that keeps on giving — spoiling the whole holiday period for your host and any other guests. Criticizing the host’s home, food (how could you), or decor was among the other bad behaviors, sitting in the top five, along with bringing a pet without asking or dragging children along to an adults-only gathering. What drives me to distraction (Image credit: Shutterstock) Having phones on the dinner table is one of my pet peeves, and I’m not alone. A solid 62% of those surveyed agree that guests should tuck their phones away during a visit. It’s no surprise that Baby Boomers were most opposed to this habit at 77%, but it spans generations, with even young Gen Zers at 52% considering screens at the table bad form. So, while my grandparents constantly enforced the “elbows off the table" rule, the survey shows that this old-school etiquette no longer matters and has been surpassed by keeping screens out of view. Other etiquette rules you need to know (Image credit: Shutterstock) Are you always late to the party? It turns out 40% do not consider arriving more than 15 minutes late impolite, but you will be frowned upon if you arrive very late without sending a courtesy text. However, keep an eye on the clock if you're invited to a Baby Boomer’s party, as 68% like guests to arrive within 15 minutes of the start time. The most taboo subject in social gatherings is discussing appearance and weight, with 55% agreeing that the topic should be off-limits. And while you won't be chastised for not taking your shoes off, four in five say it's basic etiquette, though Baby Boomers aren’t quite as bothered. One word of advice from me: if you like to keep your feet cozy, don’t turn up to your boss’s house with your slippers — that’s strictly for family-only visits in my book. articles.title: The first chapter of Denzel Washington's $500 million action trilogy is streaming on Netflix now
articles.content: The Tom's Guide verdict: 'The Equalizer' (2014) Rating: 3/5 stars Verdict: "The Equalizer" isn't Denzel Washington's best action movie, but it might be the purest expression of the Oscar winner as an action star. It has very little plot and even less time for nonsense. But it's an enjoyable watch and plays off Denzel's ability to be the strong and silent type while also letting him shoot someone dead with a nail gun. If this movie hadn't come out a month before "John Wick," I'd swear it copied the latter's bloodthirsty desire for eye-popping kills. Where to watch: Stream "The Equalizer" on Netflix " The Equalizer " might be the perfect example of "action-star Denzel." This is a Denzel Washington archetype I discussed in my previous Denzel Watchathon movie, " 2 Guns ," and it's essentially one of two roles that the legendary actor takes on. Either he's a complicated, dramatic lead dripping with gravitas, or he's a cold-blooded killer who happens to be on the right side of the morality spectrum. This action movie is undeniably in the latter camp. It reunites Denzel with Antoine Fuqua, who directed the former in " Training Day ." That was ultimately an Oscar-winning performance for Washington (and the best one of his career). Arguably, there's no better director for "action-star" Denzel to work with, save for maybe the late, great Tony Scott. Unfortunately, this cinematic reboot of a 1980s television show is no "Training Day." It's far closer to the aforementioned "2 Guns," with a lot less fun and a lot more death by corkscrew (not a euphemism). But the action set pieces themselves are well-executed, and if you're someone who loves a gnarly kill in an action movie, it's definitely worth checking out while you can stream it on Netflix . Especially if you're a fan of "John Wick." If you want to watch this movie before you read on, I have good news! It's currently streaming on Netflix , one of the best streaming services we've tested. This feels like a 'John Wick' clone despite coming out first "The Equalizer" might already be a familiar name to you, even if you've never seen the movie. It's a reboot of a 1980s TV show that was relatively shortlived. But it ultimately found a devoted fan base to merit a second attempt starring Denzel that would go on to span three movies (and generate enough interest to launch another TV show based on the '80s series). Read more Denzel Watchathon Here are some of the other Denzel Washington movies I've covered to date in my Denzel Watchathon: "Cry Freedom" (1987) "Glory" (1989) "Malcolm X" (1992) "Philadelphia" (1993) "Crimson Tide" (1995) "Remember the Titans" (2000) "Training Day" (2001) "Man on Fire" (2004) " American Gangster" (2007) "Flight" (2012) "2 Guns" (2013) Read more: Every Denzel Watchathon movie so far In this iteration, Denzel plays Robert "Bob" McCall. He's a retired Marine and former DIA officer who has ditched the life of a spy for working in a big-box home improvement store that's definitely not Home Depot. He keeps a relatively low profile, despite claiming to be a former member of Gladys Knight and the Pips, and it seems like he'll go about his days working a 9-to-5, then heading to a 24-hour diner for a cup of tea and a nice book to read. He can't escape who he really is, though. No matter how hard he tries. So when he sees that his unlikely diner buddy, Alina (Chloë Grace Moretz) — a teenage sex worker who goes by the name Teri when working — has been roughed up enough that she's in the hospital, he decides to go to the Russian mobsters that run her escort service to try to buy her freedom. If the archetype of a silent former killer looking for the quiet life but unable to escape it feels familiar, you're not alone. The entire time I'm watching "The Equalizer," I can't stop thinking about "John Wick." Unsurprisingly, Bob is almost laughed out of the building. Almost . articles.title: iPhone 18 Pro Sales Surge in China, Offsetting Decline in U.S. and Japan
articles.content: China is doing much of the heavy lifting for Apple's iPhone 18 Pro launch, with a 29% sales increase helping offset declines in the U.S. and Japan, according to Counterpoint Research . Combined global sales of the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ and ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ Max rose 3.1% during their first three weeks of availability compared with the equivalent launch period last year. U.S. sales fell 4%, while Japan recorded a 27% decline. Counterpoint attributed China's growth to better initial supply and higher prices for competing Android flagships. In the U.S., the firm said buyers perceived insufficient changes to features and design, despite additions such as the variable aperture camera . Apple raised starting prices by $100 in the U.S., bringing the Pro to $1,199 and the Pro Max to $1,299. Counterpoint pointed out that exchange rates compounded price increases in Japan. The Pro Max model's share of sales slipped from 57% to 56%, with growth in India and Southeast Asia favoring the smaller model. The tracking period predates the iPhone Duo 's launch on October 23. Counterpoint is watching whether Apple's first foldable iPhone brings in additional buyers or diverts purchases from the Pro Max. articles.content: HIFIMAN Sundara review: Cheat sheet Price: 4/5 Sound quality: 5/5 Comfort: 4/5 Durability: 3/5 Overall score: 4/5 Best for: Beginner audiophiles Reddit has many opinions — some worth your time, some not. But the HIFIMAN Sundara are some of r/audiophile and r/headphones’ most-recommended hi-fi headphones, and you know what? I agree. At just $179, they’re pretty accessible for most people. Hi-fi headphones can very quickly start costing well over $500, but not the HIFIMAN Sundara. These inconspicuous cans are comfortable, affordable, and, most importantly, sound excellent. Texture and timbre is divine, and the warm tuning makes for a non-fatiguing listen. Is this price and performance enough to make the HIFIMAN Sundara some of the best headphones ? Almost undoubtedly yes. I’ll go over everything in detail in this HIFIMAN Sundara review. HIFIMAN Sundara review: Specs Price $179 / £169 Drivers Planar magnetic Impedance 32Ω Sensitivity 92dB/1mW Headphone type Open-back Frequency response 6Hz - 75kHz Durability No IP rating Connectivity 3.5mm cable, 6.35mm adapter Multipoint connectivity N/A ANC N/A Wear detection N/A Battery life N/A Weight 12 ounces Colors Black HIFIMAN Sundara review: What I like From the $179 price tag to the sound quality, there’s a lot I like about the HIFIMAN Sundara. Sound quality (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Oh, the HIFIMAN Sundara sound like angels singing into my ears. To get the best sound, I used them with my FiiO K11 R2R DAC/Amp. With a low 32Ω impedance and sensitivity of 96dB/mW, the headphones are loud enough to power from a phone, so don’t require an amp. However, low-impedance headphones with large drivers like these perform best with stable power from an external amp, which helps the drivers move properly to avoid distortion and muddiness. The Sundara are more expansive than a hot air balloon trip across the Alps. You can feel everything — every lick of sibilance, every singer’s inhale, every pulse of bass. Instruments are separated delicately and with precision, particularly in Charlotte Gainsbourg’s “Deadly Valentine”. The atmospheric, dark alt electronic track is structured over two basslines, one a soul-inspired slap-bass and one a wriggling synth, both of which came through clearly. Gainsbourg’s smooth, buttery vocals were replicated with clarity and technical detail. This is music you feel, rather than merely listen to. (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Even heavier genres fared well, which is a pitfall some cheaper Hi-Fi cans stumble into. “Knights of Cydonia” was a propulsive, energetic inferno. The arpeggiated synths were tucked deftly underneath the harmonized vocals, and the sci-fi sound effects bounced around the back of the soundstage like they were alive. While a touch of the higher-frequency synths were lost right at the crescendo, I’m willing to overlook this for $179. Stereo imaging was also a standout, especially in “Vogue (Q-Sound Mix)” by Madonna. The soundstage was atmospheric and vast; the subtle sub-bass flickered in the background, allowing space for the finger-snap percussion. But the true excellence here was Madonna’s vocals: each whisper of “vogue” was a tangible, material (pun intended) sensation. The HIFIMAN Sundara seriously punch above their weight in terms of sound. Subtle foreshadowing, but corners have been cut elsewhere to keep the costs down. Price At $179 from Amazon U.S. and £169 from Amazon U.K , the HIFIMAN Sundara are relatively affordable, all things considered. This price makes them accessible to casual hi-fi fans or beginner audiophiles. Similar options are the FiiO FT1 Pro ($219), Sennheiser HD569 ($179), or the Sennheiser HD 560S ($199). The FiiO FT1 Pro are a little too pricey, in my opinion, so I’d recommend the Sundara over them. However, if you can spend a little more and prefer a neutral tuning, the Sennheiser HD 560S might be an overall better option. The 560S are famous in the audiophile world for a reason: they’re expansive and detailed, just like…

articles.title: AI data centers are hiking electric bills for millions — even if there's not one in your town
articles.content: The buildings are windowless, fenced, and often bigger than a shopping mall, and more of them are landing in American communities every month to feed the AI boom. The computing power behind chatbots , image generators, and the AI features now baked into your phone has to live somewhere, and that somewhere is an increasingly hungry network of data centers drawing enormous amounts of electricity from the same grid that powers your home. Data centers consumed about 4.4% of all U.S. electricity in 2023, up from 58 terawatt-hours in 2014 to 176 terawatt-hours in 2023, and the Department of Energy’s Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory projects that share could reach between 6.7% and 12% of the country’s total electricity consumption by 2028. When that much new demand shows up near your town, the cost of meeting it rarely stays with the company that created it. How data centers fuel your electricity bill (Image credit: Getty Images) The part that should concern homeowners is that a data center doesn't have to be anywhere near your house to affect your electric bill. You could live miles away from the nearest facility and still end up helping pay for the electricity infrastructure it needs. Here's why. When a massive data center connects to the power grid, utilities may need to build new power plants, substations and transmission lines to keep up with demand. Those projects cost billions, and depending on local regulations, some of that expense can be passed along to everyone who pays an electric bill. As Ari Peskoe, director of Harvard's Electricity Law Initiative, explained to NPR , those costs can be spread across businesses and households throughout the region. In other words, you don't have to use AI or live next door to a data center to help cover the costs of powering one. We're already seeing what that looks like. PJM Interconnection , which manages the electric grid for 67 million people across 13 states and Washington, D.C., holds auctions to make sure enough power will be available when demand is highest. As demand from data centers has surged, the cost of securing that power has jumped dramatically. According to Reuters , auction prices rose roughly 1,000% in two years. Prices reached a record $333.44 per megawatt-day in December 2025, although PJM's July 2026 auction came in slightly lower at $325. And those higher costs do eventually reach customers. PJM previously estimated that rising capacity costs alone could add between 1.5% and 5% to some household electricity bills. And an analysis from consulting firm ICF, reported by Reuters , warned that residential electricity rates across the region could climb between 30% and 60% by 2030. Perhaps the most striking number comes from PJM's independent market monitor, which estimated that data center demand contributed $29.4 billion to capacity auction costs across four auctions . That's not $29.4 billion added directly to homeowners' bills, but it shows just how expensive the AI boom is becoming for the electric grid. And the question now is how much of that cost should fall on the companies building these facilities, rather than the households already paying to keep the lights on. The numbers where data centers cluster (Image credit: Future) Some parts of the country are feeling the pressure more than others, especially places where data centers are being built close together. Northern Virginia is a prime example. The area is known as "Data Center Alley" because it has the largest concentration of data centers in the world. And with so many facilities drawing power from the same regional grid, keeping up with demand is becoming more expensive. The effects don't stop at the Virginia border. In neighboring Maryland, households are estimated to be paying an extra $168 to $216 a year on their electricity bills, primarily because of growing data center demand. And researchers warn that the problem could get worse. A 2026 study from NC State, Carnegie Mellon and other…

articles.title: I kept waking up at 3 a.m. until I discovered this free hidden iPhone feature — now I sleep through the night
articles.content: I've being testing sleep tech for over three years, and while most of these gadgets stop 3 a.m. wake ups and help me fall asleep fast, there's no denying that a lot come with hefty price tags. So, when I recently found myself waking up in the early hours of the morning, I was determined to find an effective but cheap solution. Luckily, I discovered a quick fix that was not only cheap but totally free — and it was hidden away on my iPhone all along. Yes, there are plenty of free iPhone sleep apps you can download, but this setting requires no sign-ups, memberships, or subscription fees. In fact, it's already on your iPhone. Here's how I used this free iPhone feature to stop waking up at 3 a.m. Plus, sleep experts (including a psychologist and neurologist) explain why it works and how you can use it to suit your own sleep needs. The iPhone feature that stops my 3 a.m. wake ups I'm an incredibly light sleeper, meaning I get jolted awake by even the slightest sound. From a creaking door to a TV playing in the next room, any break in the silence (no matter how brief or quiet) can fragment my sleep and leave me awake at 3 a.m. Usually, I use the best sleep earbuds or my trusty Loop Quiet 2 earplugs , but I had to give my ear canals a break after I tested a pair of chunky ANC earbuds that were, in hindsight, way too big for a prolonged period of time. So, I had to find another way to block out noise that wouldn't cause further irritation to my ears, and that's when I discovered the free iPhone feature. (Image credit: Future) The Background Sounds setting on my iPhone is specifically designed to play background sounds to mask unwanted environmental noise. Along with providing a coping mechanism for those who experience tinnitus, it also minimises nocturnal distractions for light sleepers. This isn't my first brush with noise-masking sounds, as I tested and loved the LectroFan Evo White Noise Machine . However, a recent move meant I had to jettison the white noise machine (along with the myriad other sleep products I've tested and couldn't take with me). What makes this feature so great is that it's free, always easily accessible for iPhone users, and provides a variety of background sounds that are not just limited to fan sounds . This includes balanced noise ( white noise ), bright noise ( pink noise ), dark noise ( brown noise ), and nature sounds such as ocean waves, crackling fire, rainfall, streams, and even a plane. You may be wondering why I like these background sounds so much when I stated above that I need peace and quiet to sleep. However, when silence isn't available, a continuous and consistent sound is the next best thing. "The best sound for sleep is usually one that feels steady and non-intrusive while gently masking environmental noise," explains board-certified neurologist Dr. Lynette Gogol . "The key factor is whether the sound masks environmental disturbances without drawing attention to itself." How to set up and choose Background Sounds for sleep Accessing the iPhone feature is simple. Just go to your Settings app, and scroll down to find Accessibility . Select Audio & Visual , and from there you can find Background Sounds . Toggle this feature on and click Sound to see a full menu of different background sounds. Select the one you prefer. After you pick the best sound for your sleep, you can then adjust the volume and even set a timer. Just select Stop Sounds with a Timer and toggle the timer on. You can either set the timer so the background stops at a specific time (for example, 6 a.m. to coincide with your wake-up alarm) or after a certain amount of time (for example, two hours after it begins). Just go to your Settings app, and scroll down to find Accessibility Future Select Audio & Visual, and from there you can find Background Sounds. articles.title: iPhone Duo 2 is inevitable — and these are the 7 things we want to see
articles.content: After years of waiting the iPhone Duo has finally arrived, and as positive as reception has been to Apple's first foldable, it is far from a perfect phone . The Duo is definitely an excellent first attempt, but there are some things about the phone we would change. While there isn't much Apple can do about that now, it does mean there are plenty of opportunities to upgrade the inevitable iPhone Duo 2. We know it's coming at some point, and the insane demand for the foldable means Apple is going to want the sequel to be ready as soon as possible. With that in mind, here are seven things we want Apple to do with the iPhone Duo 2. Add Face ID (Image credit: Tom's Guide) One of the things people are most annoyed about was that the iPhone Duo was missing Face ID. It's been a staple part of Apple flagships for almost a decade, and the idea that it was missing directly conflicted with Apple's long-standing claims that Face ID was a much more secure system than Touch ID. It's unclear why the foldable is missing Face ID, but the good news is that the follow-up should come with Apple's trademark facial recognition system. According to Mark Gurman, Apple has already started testing a version of the Duo that features Face ID support , and that it should be part of an under display camera. It's unclear if that means the cover display camera will also be under-display, or if we'll only see hidden Face ID. Give us a telephoto lens (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Apple makes some of the best camera phones, and offers what it calls "optical quality" zoom on the Duo's main camera, but that doesn't make up for a dedicated telephoto lens. We checked, and compared to the iPhone 18 Pro Max, the quality of magnified photos is so much worse on the iPhone Duo. It is possible to have a telephoto lens on a wide foldable, even if Apple and Samsung have decided to go without. Xiaomi's 18 Fold has a triple-lens camera, complete with a 50MP telephoto lens capable of 3x optical magnification. If Xiaomi can do it, so can Apple, and it would help elevate the iPhone Duo 2's camera capabilities far beyond what's currently on offer. More optimized apps (Image credit: Tom's Guide) One of the main problems with the iPhone Duo is that the app optimization is pretty terrible . This isn't exactly Apple's fault, and it mainly stems from the fact developers have been spoiled by set display sizes and aspect ratios for many years — meaning the uniquely-shaped and transformable iPhone Duo is automatically at a disadvantage. There are a lot of optimized apps on offer, but there are still plenty more that aren't, and that needs to change and fast. Because a lack of optimized apps will make some users wonder why they bothered to spend $2,000 on a foldable when you can't make full use of the screen. So Apple needs to push those developers to better optimize well ahead of the iPhone Duo 2 launch. Because what good is having a walled garden if you can't push developers to support all your devices? Better display colors (Image credit: Tom's Guide) While many people may be critical of the fact the iPhone Duo is only available in Black or White, there's a bigger coloring issue that needs to be fixed for the Duo 2. I'm talking about the picture quality on the foldable screen which, thanks to the nano-texture display, has much more muted colors than most people would expect (or like). While this issue seems to stem from the light-diffusing nano-texture layer, it's something Apple really needs to sort out going forward. Displays are one of the most important parts of a foldable phone, and offering such an expensive device with even slightly muted colors on the big display is not a good look. A less weighty design (Image credit: Tom's Guide) The iPhone Duo is a heavy thing, and at 8.96 ounces it's actually the heaviest iPhone Apple has ever made. In direct contrast, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra , which is a larger device, is 7.58 ounces, while the passport-shaped Z Fold 8 is just 7.09…

articles.title: This free creative app is like Internet Archive meets Pinterest
articles.content: Do you remember, as a kid, going through a stack of old magazines and clipping out the sections that you liked? There was an art to it. Whether you were in class or just making some decorations for your wall at home, it was important to find clips that expressed your personality—pictures you thought were interesting or cool or that in some way said something about you. And it was fun to find sentences to put out of context, or even to cut out individual letters to create your own custom messages. But, much as some of us around here may still love them , physical magazines aren’t as omnipresent as they used to be. So how can you recreate that feeling today—and find new ways it can be useful or even just plain enjoyable in your adult life? This tip originally appeared in the free Cool Tools newsletter from The Intelligence . Get the next issue in your inbox and get ready to discover all sorts of awesome tech treasures! Your modern-day collage experience ​Clipart Studio​ is a website that simulates the experience of cutting up magazines to make a collage. ➜ You can page through real vintage magazines, virtually “cut” what you want, and put everything together in any way that suits your fancy. ⌚ You’ll need a mere minute or two to explore the site. Just open the website and get started. In the left panel, you’ll find six random magazines, sourced from the Internet Archive​ . You can browse by topic or click the little die icon to get six more random titles. ✅ Click a magazine, and you can start flipping pages—just the way you remember. When you see something you like, use the virtual knife to cut it out, then place it on your board. Keep doing this as long as you like. Clipart Studio brings old-fashioned magazine collages into the digital age. ☝️ There’s a bit more here, too. You can search for images, sourced from Wikimedia Commons. Or you can drag an image over from your own computer, if you want to make sure your cat (or child, coworker, or whatever the case may be) is featured. With sources from the Internet Archive and Wikimedia Commons, you’ve got plenty of material to work with. The possibilities are practically endless, whether you end up sharing your creation, using it for some social media purpose, or even just enjoying it yourself and not trying to turn it into anything more. (Side note: The site was made by a designer named ​Sami Smith​ , who has a knack for creating fun projects like this. Check out her ​version of Wikipedia running on an imaginary Windows XP desktop​ for another memorable retro-tech adventure. ) Clipart Studio works ​in any web browser​ , on any device. It’s free, and there’s no advertising, either. Your collage is stored in your own local browser, meaning it’s entirely private (though you can optionally share it for a public gallery, if you want). Treat yourself to all sorts of brain-boosting goodies like this with the free Cool Tools newsletter —starting with an instant introduction to an incredible audio app that’ll tune up your days in truly delightful ways.

articles.title: Cisco Gives Engineer Unlimited AI Tokens To Rewrite Legacy Code
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Fortune: Gen Z can't catch a break. Entry-level jobs are vanishing; some 40% of bosses say they plan to hire fewer grads because AI can do the job cheaper, and young workers are routinely slammed for showing up late and refusing to put in overtime for free. Cisco's president and chief product officer Jeetu Patel isn't buying it -- he's just handed one of the company's biggest jobs to a 27-year-old he found hidden in the org chart "five levels" below him. "I've given him unlimited tokens because he's going to refactor code," Patel told Fortune at a small roundtable dinner. "So I'm like, you can go, you can go nuts." The "him" is Padmanabhan Krishnamurthy, or "Paddy," as Patel affectionately calls him. He joined Cisco in 2025 after the $429 billion tech giant acquired EzDubs, the real-time translation startup Krishnamurthy cofounded in 2023. And despite coming in as a former founder with CEO experience, he was, in Patel's words, "buried away in the organization doing something unstrategic." That changed when Patel dropped into Cisco's San Francisco office, and the pair got talking. Krishnamurthy reckoned he could rewrite Cisco's legacy code with a two-person team. Patel says even the most AI-forward people on his own team weren't thinking that way. So he has given himself four weeks to prove it, with the final goal of rewriting 98% of Cisco's legacy code within 24 months. Now, he's on the hunt for more Paddys: young hires who will "challenge the system and the status quo," or, as he puts it, be "an energizer bunny that just goes out and kind of revs everyone up." "The only way for us to keep accelerating is to make sure we're surrounded by people with a broad range of experience," said Patel. "Roughly one-third of my team is experienced, scaled operators who understand how the Cisco engine works. The second third are systems thinkers from the market who bring the outside-in perspective. And the final third is made of entrepreneurial founders, CEOs, and engineers who are AI-native who operate in founder mode." "Either of these groups by themselves aren't nearly as potent as when all three work together. It's what creates magic." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: The latest Apple Watch update promises better treadmill workout tracking — so I tested it
articles.content: Back when Apple announced watchOS 27 back in June earlier this year, there was one new feature that piqued my interest more than the promise of a smarter version of Siri or a Workout Buddy that now operated more standalone. Apple revealed that it was delivering more accurate distance tracking during walks and treadmill runs. It’s primarily doing that by making improvements to the algorithms that help to calculate the distance covered when you step onto that belt. It's website states that 'improved motion tracking algorithms help measure the distance of your treadmill runs and walks more precisely straight from your wrist.' As a runner that does his fair share of runs on a treadmill (and not just because it’s got cold outside — treadmill running is great for specific pacing and incline drills), I liked the prospect that the best smartwatch ’s indoor activity credentials could now match its very solid outdoor performance — which I tested on the London marathon course’s infamous GPS black spots . So, has Apple actually managed to deliver more accurate distance tracking for indoor runners? I’ve been spending the last couple of months testing the feature across the best Apple Watches — including the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 — to find out. How I tested (Image credit: Getty Images) I began my testing using the beta versions of watchOS 27 running on the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and the Apple Watch Series 11. When watchOS 27 was given a public release, I also strapped on the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and the Watch Series 12 to see how Apple’s latest smartwatches fared indoors. I didn’t have my own treadmill (or indeed, have the room to house one), so I relied on the treadmill at my gym. While I did my best to stick to the same treadmill for these test runs, that wasn’t always possible. That did mean I’d be stepping onto treadmills of various conditions and belt wear, which does have an impact on the reliability and accuracy of the treadmill distance tracking feature. With the Apple Watch strapped alone to one wrist, I had a Coros watch on the other paired to the Coros Pod 2. This foot-worn pod is designed to track distance, among other metrics, and was an additional source of data that could offer a more reliable picture of my running distance than the motion sensors that usually do that from the wrist. I used the foot-worn pod as a control device, the same way we use the best heart rate monitors to test the readings from smartwatches. With watches on wrists and the pod on my feet, I captured a range of runs covering different paces and distances. That included short one-mile test runs, steady hour-long runs and interval runs during which I mixed up my pace. I stuck to the same incline for all runs and used Apple’s own Workout app to track the workout. Apple suggests tracking an outdoor run of at least 20 minutes to calibrate the watch and help those algorithms do a better job of understanding your stride length, and in turn, deliver more accurate distance tracking. I did that with each Watch I tested. The results (Image credit: Ljupco Smokovski / Shutterstock) On the early runs in my testing using the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and the Series 11, I found a difference of about 300 metres (0.3km) from the distances the treadmill and Coros Pod 2 reported. If I’m looking at that difference in terms of a longer distance race such as a marathon, that’s quite a small difference. If we’re looking at that difference over a shorter distance race such as a 5km, then it might be the kind of difference that mattered. When I switched to testing with the publicly available version of watchOS 27 with the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and the Series 12, there tended to be a difference between the treadmill and watches of roughly 200 metres. Again, that’s a very good performance and a small difference when you’re banking a longer run. articles.title: Someone found their lost Bose bud in a field of gravel using ChatGPT, and it's genius
articles.content: Imagine the scene. You're in the park with your family, you're running to catch up with them, and your earbud case falls out of your pocket, scattering your earbuds. You find one but the other has vanished and all you can see is gravel. Who ya gonna call? For Just-a-fungi893 on Reddit , the answer is: ChatGPT. "I spent a solid 10 minutes searching, knowing there's basically no way I'm going to find a tiny white earbud in a sea of white gravel, especially with the sun setting," they explained. "I use ChatGPT for A LOT of stuff, and it suddenly dawned on me to ask it for help instead of pointlessly scanning the area myself." Five minutes later, earbud and owner were reunited, with ChatGPT steering him towards the exact point in the relevant photo. It's not because ChatGPT has magic powers, but because LLMs are really good at spotting tiny things in big pictures: earbuds in gravel, needles in haystacks, indicators of tumors in X-rays. It's all pattern recognition. ChatGPT found my lost earbud from r/ChatGPT It's time to embrace our AI overlords vs no, it isn't As fun as the story is — I'd never have thought of taking a photo and feeding it to a chatbot; it's smart thinking — one of the other comments on the Reddit thread made me laugh: Mindless-Apricot-236 responded that they once lost a screw outdoors, uploaded a picture to ChatGPT and "asked the oracle to help me find it. It said it found it. Showed me the picture... It just modified the original picture and put a random screw on it lol" Other commenters had suggestions that didn't involve AI at all, such as 4-jr1's "how about next time you just open Spotify and listen for the one rock among hundreds that sings out loud" — although that wouldn't work if the headphones weren't on and paired; I have Bose QuietComfort earbuds and they don't turn on until they're in my ears — and SpehlingAirer's "When this kinda thing happens to me I turn on my phone's flashlight and bring it low to the ground pointing almost horizontally. The way the light reflects off the common background (gravel, carpet, grass, etc) and the way it reflects off the glossy plastic are often different enough to help spot it quickly." And of course many of the best earbuds have some variation of Find My, enabling you to locate them from your phone. But it's nice to know that all those years we've been identifying bicycles, stairs and traffic lights in website CAPTCHAs has paid off: computer vision has become really incredible. As to whether it's reliable, I'll just leave this, by AnalogAngeleno, here: "I tried something similar at a used bookstore. Took a photo of the shelve and asked it to help look for books since they were not in any kind of order. Unfortunately it started making up books that were not even there." Still, you'll get different results depending on the type of task and the model you're using — evidently, this one worked well enough, and seems like a good tip to keep in mind for your own earbud emergency.

articles.title: Anduril wants to become a laptop maker — drone and defense giant partners with Qualcomm to build new BlueChip devices, all made in the US
articles.content: Anduril plans to open BlueChip laptop orders in 2027 with Qualcomm BlueChip prototypes source 90% of component procurement costs from American and allied suppliers Anduril expects its laptops to cost 20% more than comparable devices Anduril Industries has revealed plans to enter the laptop market through a partnership with Qualcomm, with plans to begin accepting orders for its BlueChip computers in 2027. The defense technology company, best known for its military drones , intends to reduce reliance on overseas suppliers as it develops the new laptop line. However, its current sourcing figures show that eliminating foreign suppliers remains a future objective rather than an existing achievement. BlueChip begins with American manufacturing The company has developed working prototypes featuring Qualcomm Snapdragon X Series processors, which will power the laptops. Anduril says suppliers in the United States and allied countries account for 90% of the procurement cost of the components used in its prototypes. The company already sources several parts locally, including batteries, computer enclosures and display glass. Its strategy also involves using metals that American industries can extract, refine and process at commercial scale. “Other companies might design their computers in the U.S., Anduril makes them here,” said Palmer Luckey, founder of Anduril Industries, in a company video. “We’re making parts out of metals that the U.S. knows how to extract, knows how to refine, knows how to process, and knows how to mill at scale at a reasonable price; and that goes for the entire laptop. The same thing goes for the battery technology.” The company says the laptop is designed to withstand demanding environments, with replaceable upper and lower shells that allow users to customize its configuration. These interchangeable panels could accommodate additions such as solar panels, specialised fabric materials and service insignia, according to Anduril’s video. The design also allows flat phased-array antennas to be integrated directly into the laptop’s chassis, potentially supporting specialised applications in demanding operating environments. Anduril estimates that producing a fully American-made laptop could cost 20% more than a comparable device, potentially limiting its appeal to ordinary consumers. Therefore, it appears to be focused on customers with specific security requirements, including government agencies, military organizations, emergency responders, and public safety departments. These buyers may accept higher prices to address concerns about hardware security and supply chain reliability. A domestic supply chain remains difficult Anduril acknowledges that producing complete laptops requires more than processors and selected parts. Circuit boards, displays, batteries, and other essential components remain heavily dependent on foreign suppliers, complicating efforts to eliminate reliance on these suppliers. “BlueChip will take a phased approach, beginning with expanding domestic sourcing and manufacturing, progressing toward eliminating reliance on foreign suppliers, and ultimately establishing an end-to-end American supply chain,” the company said in its announcement. The project comes as semiconductor investment grows in the United States, including TSMC’s facilities in Arizona and Samsung’s site in Taylor, Texas. These projects could improve access to locally fabricated chips, but they do not guarantee a domestic source for every part needed to assemble a laptop. Taiwan has also planned support for smaller companies supplying TSMC through industrial parks in the United States. Such initiatives could give BlueChip access to additional suppliers, although their eventual contribution to the laptop’s production remains unclear. Via Tom's Hardware

articles.title: Sam Altman says OpenAI won't slow its math and science paper barrage
articles.content: OpenAI will keep pushing AI’s scientific discoveries, Sam Altman says Some researchers are excited by the ‘fantastic’ breakthroughs But others warn that the pace of change is ‘psychologically taxing’ One of the promises that huge AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have made is that their machine learning models will help to solve some of the oldest problems in math and science. The pace of their discoveries has left many experts struggling to keep up, but OpenAI’s Sam Altman just has just said there’s much more in store — and not everyone is happy about that. Speaking on the Cheeky Pint podcast , Altman outlined his belief that “Humanity deserves fundamental knowledge, and we should not be sitting on a major fundamental science discovery.” That rationale is why OpenAI has published breakthrough after breakthrough in these fields, knocking down some of the oldest and toughest problems that have troubled great thinkers for years. But the way in which the company has set out its results has drawn criticism for often inadequate attributions and questionable verification processes. While Altman acknowledged that, saying on the podcast that “I do have empathy for the method” and saying OpenAI’s quest for mathematical challenges did “get out of control” at times, he suggested that there’s much more to come. Asked if the firm has anymore unpublished breakthroughs in its vaults, he replied “We do. Of course.” That’s led to accusations that, far from giving people “fundamental knowledge,” OpenAI is gatekeeping important discoveries. And there’s another problem: the sheer scale of the new research is swamping academics. For instance, Wired has noted that the company recently “dumped 722 manuscripts on 400 problems on GitHub,” leaving the scientific community to pick through the enormous mass of information. And the impact of having the most important work in your life suddenly undercut by a machine is “psychologically taxing for many people,” said Thore Husfeldt of the IT University of Copenhagen. Husfeldt added that there is “a lot of doom and gloom, because every week, or every second week, the results announced by AI just annihilate the ongoing research projects of many people.” Obliterating entire fields of research (Image credit: Shutterstock) AI models’ ability to solve thorny problems was keenly demonstrated when it apparently disproved the exponential time hypothesis (ETH), which argued that the effort needed to solve a problem increases with its complexity. That’s upended countless theories that assumed that ETH was correct and left many experts scrambling to catch up. As Linköping University professor Peter Jonsson told Wired, although AI’s tendency to undermine years-long research can be irksome, “at the same time, we learn a lot from it. And this is what science is about.” UC Santa Barbara professor Daniel Lokshtanov aptly described the mood among many scientists and mathematicians, saying “It’s just a giant bomb dropped into the middle of the field,” he says. “It’s really cool and terrible at the same time.” For Husfeldt, meanwhile, the discovery is “fantastic.” He added: “Being a mathematician is a lot like stumbling about in a completely dark room. It’s like somebody just illuminated an entire subfield in floodlights of knowledge, and now we just run around like overexcited bunnies and look at all the nooks and crannies that we can suddenly explore. So it’s a super exciting time.” In the case of the ETH theory, OpenAI’s work has not been peer reviewed or independently verified. But it’s clear that AI research is creating generational changes in many areas — and overturning entire fields of study in an instant, with all the excitement and chaos that comes with that. Jonsson fittingly summed the situation up, saying: “I don’t care if it’s a human-written proof, or it’s written by AI, or if an alien transmitted this proof to us. If it’s true, then we must simply use it in the future.”

articles.title: Washington governor rips Microsoft over TV ad in leaked audio
articles.content: Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, speaking at an event in Olympia in June, called out Microsoft last week over a TV ad from a PAC the company has helped fund. (Office of the Governor Photo) Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson called out Microsoft for bankrolling a political action committee responsible for a TV ad describing state government as broken, according to newly leaked audio from a Seattle Chamber leadership conference last week. Remarks at the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce’s Regional Leadership Conference, held at the Suncadia resort near Cle Elum, Wash., are supposed to be off the record. But The Washington Observer , an independent newsletter on state politics, published the audio Friday , saying it was obtained from an unnamed source. In the audio, Ferguson zeroed in on a line near the start of the ad — that in Washington, “it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.” The governor repeated the words “it used to be” for emphasis, in a tone of disbelief. “What’s up with that?” Ferguson asked the crowd of business and government leaders. “First, does anyone else in this room believe that? I sure as hell don’t.” “I talk to people every day who have that idea, that dream. They’re chasing it and they’re getting it,” he said. He cited the record $3.5 billion that Seattle-area startups raised in the third quarter, more than triple the same period a year ago, according to PitchBook data. The Microsoft relationship: Ferguson, who noted that he had worked as a lawyer for Microsoft, said he loves the company and respects what it does. But he seemed especially peeved that the ad ran during the Seattle Seahawks game, where it reached people across the state and those from elsewhere who might want to come here and start a company. “If we’re partners, partners should treat partners like partners, right?” he said. He asked the room to imagine him running a multimillion-dollar ad criticizing Microsoft. “You guys would think I lost my mind if I did that,” he said. Ferguson called Microsoft a key partner and a member of his economic roundtable, and said he works well with the company. “But it works both ways,” he said. Ferguson acknowledged that the state has problems. “Are there challenges? Sure,” he said. But he said he didn’t think the ad was “helpful for where we all want to go.” He told the crowd he welcomes constructive feedback, but asked business leaders to think about how they communicate, and to talk up the state’s workforce, economy and startup funding along with its challenges. “What we have here is so bloody special,” he said. Ferguson, who took office in January 2025, also reminded the room that he isn’t going anywhere. “I plan on being governor for a long time,” he said, adding that he works with all of them, “Microsoft included.” The Observer noted that $10 million, roughly what the group has left to spend, would be a good start on a campaign to run someone else for governor in 2028. The newsletter said it released just the audio from a video of Ferguson’s remarks, to protect its source. Among those in the audience was Michael Mattmiller, who represents Microsoft in Olympia. He and Ferguson “kinda-sorta hugged it out afterward,” the Observer reported. Mattmiller declined to comment to the Observer, and Ferguson’s office didn’t respond to the publication. GeekWire has contacted Microsoft and the governor’s office for comment. Who’s behind the ad: The campaign comes from Washington Needs to Compete, a PAC funded in large part by Microsoft and its current and former executives. The group has raised about $13.8 million, according to state campaign finance records , including more than $5 million directly from Microsoft. Microsoft CEO Satya…

articles.title: Once again, NASA is asking for ideas to rescue Hubble from certain death
articles.content: The Hubble Space Telescope still shines in the eyes of astronomers after 36 years in orbit, but it is not as nimble as it once was. Left alone, the observatory will plunge back into the atmosphere in the early-to-mid-2030s, closing the book on one of the most famous scientific instruments of the century. NASA last raised the orbit of Hubble in 2002, when the Space Shuttle Columbia visited the observatory for a servicing mission. The final shuttle servicing flight in 2009 did not reboost the telescope's orbit, and with the retirement of the shuttle fleet two years later, Hubble has steadily lost altitude with no way to stave off eventual destruction. The space agency released a Request For Information (RFI) on Thursday asking commercial companies for ideas on how to reboost, service, or a controlled disposal of Hubble. Responses are due November 30. Specifically, NASA is looking for information about companies' current and near-term capabilities for capturing Hubble and boosting it to an altitude of at least 373 miles (600 km), enhancing the telescope's performance, or guiding Hubble to a controlled reentry. articles.title: HomeView Software 27.2: Wallpapers, Control Center, and More
articles.content: Apple today released HomeView Software 27.2, which is the software that runs on the upcoming HomeView device set to launch on November 13. The HomeView was announced earlier in October, but the early software release gives us a look at features like wallpapers and reveals a few tidbits we didn't previously know. Wallpapers There are 20 default wallpapers to choose from on HomeView, with a range of colors. Users will also likely be able to set their own photo wallpaper. The HomeView uses faces, but the wallpapers may be shown on the Home Screen . View all 20 photos in the full article → Face Editing Guilherme Rambo shared an image of the HomeView's face editing interface, where users can choose the design they want to use on the HomeView's Lock Screen. Of course I had to virtualize a HomeView 😅 First look at the face editing UI. https://t.co/3t03FVmuP3 — Guilherme Rambo (@_inside) October 30, 2026 Hello Screen At startup, the HomeView will show the familiar "Hello" text. Hello! https://t.co/pXdUR21Gev — Guilherme Rambo (@_inside) October 30, 2026 Control Center A HomeView setup animation shows Control Center on the HomeView. HomeView setup animation found in HomeView Software 27.2 https://t.co/k4gCHNV3bY — Aaron (@aaronp613) October 30, 2026 Light and Dark Mode As with other Apple devices, the HomeView will have Light Mode and Dark Mode options, with the device able to swap between modes automatically based on time of day. Snoopy The HomeView has a bunch of different Snoopy animations if you pick the Snoopy face. Here are the Snoopy videos from the HomeView 🧵 https://t.co/hrRxPlmVSS — Aaron (@aaronp613) October 30, 2026 Launcher Unlike iOS, HomeView doesn't use SpringBoard. It has a new launcher called BreadBoard , and the process for its Control Center UI is called CupBoard. iOS 26 There is a hidden HomeView Software 26 graphic in the update, which adds to evidence that Apple wanted to release the HomeView earlier but had to wait on Siri AI. Apple also appears to have been testing the interface on a sixth-generation iPad mini before launch. HomeView Software contains this image, adding more indiciation it was initially going to ship with HomeView Software 26 last year https://t.co/yV1a1lbJcr — Aaron (@aaronp613) October 30, 2026 The HomeView is priced at $299, and it can be pre-ordered from Apple's website. It will launch alongside the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K on November 13. Related Roundup: Apple HomeView Buyer's Guide: HomeView (Buy Now) Related Forum: HomePod, HomeView, CarPlay – Home & Auto Tech This article, " HomeView Software 27.2: Wallpapers, Control Center, and More " first appeared on MacRumors.com Discuss this article in our forums

articles.title: Apple Is Entering Its Slop Era
articles.content: In an opinion piece for 404 Media, Matthew Gault argues that Apple has entered its "slop era," abandoning its reputation for innovative hardware in favor of recycled ideas and questionable design choices. Here's an excerpt: My ears perked up when I heard Apple's new foldable phones were cracking. I licked my lips when the company announced it's releasing a touch-screen laptop. This was a company that once charged $19 for a polishing cloth, asked $200 for a VESA mount, and sold $700 wheels for the Mac Pro. Now it's borrowing tired ideas from its competitors and launching hardware its previous leaders rejected. The once dominant company is struggling to find its feet in an AI-driven post-Tim Cook world. John Ternus is the new CEO -- a 25 year veteran of the company with a track record of pushing harebrained hardware schemes like the much reviled Touch Bar and lawsuit inducing butterfly keyboard. With Ternus at the helm, I feel there's a good chance Apple's best days are behind it, that it will have to make do with less, that it's declasse. Apple, blindsided by AI and relying on crowdpleasing hardware gimmicks, is downwardly mobile. It's in its slop era. The company that once asked consumers to "Think Different" is now releasing hardware that's just like everything else on the market. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.author: BeauHD

articles.title: Managing Amazon Bedrock costs end to end: A playbook for FinOps and platform teams
articles.content: Cost management for generative AI is a shared responsibility between the teams that build applications and the teams accountable for cloud spend. Many teams start by comparing per-model token rates and asking application teams to shorten prompts. Those steps help, but they don’t answer the questions that finance and engineering leaders ask as usage scales: which team spent this, on which workload, and was that spend inside an approved budget? Agentic workloads make those questions more pressing. A conversational assistant typically issues one model invocation per user turn. An agentic workflow, such as an AI coding assistant that plans a change, reads files, calls tools, and iterates, issues many invocations per task and carries a larger context on each one. Token consumption therefore scales with the degree of autonomy you grant the workflow and the size of the context it carries, rather than with the number of user interactions. Because consumption is a function of how a workload is designed and operated, cost management for generative AI is an architectural and operational discipline. Published averages are a poor substitute for your own numbers: use the AWS Pricing Calculator and the Amazon Bedrock pricing page to model rates, and use Step 2 of this post to measure what your workloads actually consume. The fix isn’t a cheaper model or a smaller prompt. It’s an operating model: a repeatable loop that attributes every dollar to an owner, makes every request observable, alerts on and enforces budgets before overspend compounds, optimizes the platform defaults that drive most waste, and reviews the whole system on a cadence. In this post, you learn how to manage Amazon Bedrock cost in five steps. You attribute every dollar to an owner, make every request observable, control spend with budgets and enforcement, optimize the platform defaults that drive most avoidable spend, and operate a review cadence that turns data into decisions. This approach is built from AWS building blocks, and you can customize it and apply it to your own environment. The post is written for two audiences: FinOps practitioners who own attribution, chargeback, budgets, and anomaly review, and platform engineering teams who own logging, request metadata, enforcement, and routing defaults. The operating model in one view Five stages, run as a loop. Attribute: every Amazon Bedrock dollar lands on an identity, team, and application in the billing pipeline. Observe: every request is logged with enough metadata to explain what generated the spend. Enforce: budgets have teeth, with alerts at minimum and hard blocks where the risk demands them. Optimize: the platform defaults (model routing, caching, token limits) remove waste centrally instead of asking every team to be careful. Operate: a small scorecard and a review cadence turn the data into decisions. FinOps leads stages one and five. Platform engineering leads two through four. The review is joint. The stages are sequenced deliberately. Each one depends on the ones before it, and teams that jump straight to optimization without attribution and observability are guessing. Figure 1: The five-stage operating model, run as a continuous loop Stage 1: Attribute every dollar You can’t manage what you can’t attribute, and everything downstream (chargeback, budgets, enforcement, anomaly detection) depends on this stage. The foundation is the granular cost attribution of Amazon Bedrock (see Introducing granular cost attribution for Amazon Bedrock ): Amazon Bedrock automatically attributes inference costs to the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal that made the call, across all models, with no resources to manage. The caller’s ARN lands in the line_item_iam_principal column of the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) 2.0 , and coverage spans IAM users, roles, federated identities, and API keys. Setup is four steps: Turn on IAM principal data in your CUR 2.0 data export. Tag your IAM principals with…

articles.title: Flesh-eating screwworms spread to third state and are attacking pets
articles.content: For a genuine fright this Halloween, you can turn your gaze to the southern border, where ravenous, flesh-eating maggots are festering and have taken to eating people's pets. This week, the country's New World Screwworm (NWS) infestation spread to a third state, Arizona, which joins New Mexico and Texas in being plagued by the horrifying parasites. To date, 74 animal cases have been identified in the US since the flies re-invaded the country in June. The flies lay hundreds of eggs in wounds and moist orifices of animals, and the resulting voracious maggots feast on their victims. The maggots resemble screws and tortuously bore and twist into living flesh, causing severe, sometimes fatal wounds, before dropping to the ground to develop into adults. Read full article Comments
articles.author: Beth Mole

articles.title: Oh captain, our captain: Ars staff remembers Patrick Stewart
articles.content: Along with the rest of the world, we at Ars are mourning Sir Patrick Stewart —the beloved award-winning actor best known as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men franchise—who died yesterday at the age of 86. A statement released by Stewart's representatives said: We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia. He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all. We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace. Through the actor's X account , the family has requested that, in lieu of flowers, memorial contributions be made to the Johns Hopkins Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center Fund and the Alzheimer’s Foundation of America Caregiver Resources . articles.author: Jennifer Ouellette

articles.title: Apple Alerts Stores to iPhone Duo's Display Cracking Issue
articles.content: In a memo shared with Apple Stores and Apple Authorized Service Providers this week, and later obtained by MacRumors , Apple provided technicians with guidance on how to diagnose and address the iPhone Duo's inner display cracking issue. If a customer reports the issue, Apple advised technicians to inspect the iPhone Duo and repair or replace it in accordance with their standard procedures. While the instructions themselves are straightforward, the fact that Apple issued an internal memo suggests the issue is widespread enough to warrant official guidance. Apple's memo said the issue affects a small number of iPhone Duo units, which is consistent with what it said in a public statement on Monday. "We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units," said Apple, in a statement shared with MacRumors . If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement." You can get support on Apple's website or by calling 1-800-APL-CARE in the U.S. and Canada. Apple said most iPhone Duo units are not susceptible to this issue and that impacted units appear to exhibit the defects rather quickly after usage. Apple said there is no iPhone Duo recall, and the company has yet to launch a public-facing repair program on its website for this issue. Almost immediately after the iPhone Duo began arriving to customers a week ago, a handful of early adopters reported that the device's inner display had cracked , resulting in lines appearing down the middle and towards the right side of the screen. The electronics repair website iFixit completed an iPhone Duo teardown and said that the issue is likely related to a defective hinge on affected units. However, Apple has yet to comment on the underlying cause of the issue.
