articles.title: Madrona Prize goes to UW research on agents that shrink AI models to run on small chips
articles.content: Madrona Prize honorees with representatives from Madrona at the Allen School Research Showcase. From left: Karan Mehandru, Chris Picardo and Joe Horseman of Madrona; Zhihan Zhang, Madrona Prize winner; Tanush Yadav, first runner-up; Jacob Morrison of Madrona and the Allen School; and Phoebe Riser and Baxter Black of Madrona. (Photo by Kristine White) A University of Washington project that uses AI agents to squeeze AI models onto tiny devices — such as a solar-powered camera that spots elk in the wild — won the Madrona Prize at the Allen School’s annual Research Showcase on Thursday. Seattle venture capital firm Madrona has awarded the prize since 2006 to Allen School student projects that combine strong research with commercial potential. The winners were chosen from among the student posters presented at the evening event on the UW campus. Zhihan Zhang explains his Madrona Prize-winning research on using AI agents to fit AI models onto small chips. (Photo by Kristine White) Zhihan Zhang, a PhD student in the Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, presented the winning project . It tests whether AI agents can do a job that experts now do by hand: shrinking AI models and tuning device software to run on small, low-power chips with tight limits on memory, power and heat. In the team’s tests, leading AI models failed at the task without feedback from real hardware. The team built a system that let the agent load its work onto real hardware, measure the results and try again. With that feedback, the agent beat human experts within seven rounds. The researchers used the approach on two real-world projects: an elk-detection camera trap, which needed its vision model shrunk by 250 times, and a wearable device that records children’s speech for child development research. The team released its benchmark, called Embedded Arena , as open-source code. Allen School faculty members Shwetak Patel, Vikram Iyer, Natasha Jaques and Kurtis Heimerl also worked on the project. Other collaborators: Alexander Metzger, Jiuyang Lyu, Chun-Cheng Chang, Jiayi Shao, Yujia Liu, Emmanuel Azuh Mensah, Edward Wang and Gregory D. Abowd. Keisuke Kamahori with his VibeSys poster, winner of the People’s Choice award. (Photo by Kristine White) The People’s Choice award went to Keisuke Kamahori for VibeSys, a project that uses AI agents to write custom software for a specific chip and task, then keep improving it, instead of relying on general-purpose tools built for common setups. Its first application, VibeServe , writes the behind-the-scenes software that takes requests from users and runs them through an AI model. On Amazon’s Trainium2 chips, the software it built handled up to 2.7 times as much work as an existing system. Shihang (Vic) Li and Allen School faculty members Simon Peter and Baris Kasikci also worked on the project. Tanush Yadav, first runner-up for the Madrona Prize, with his VideoNet poster. (Photo by Kristine White) The first runner-up for the Madrona Prize , Tanush Yadav, presented VideoNet , a test of how well AI models recognize specific actions in video, such as a particular bouldering move or a type of surgical stitch. It covers more than 1,000 actions across 38 fields. Leading AI models struggle with it compared to ordinary people. Shown three examples, people improved their accuracy by about 14 percentage points, while AI models improved by about 3 percentage points. Allen School faculty members Ali Farhadi, Hanna Hajishirzi and Ranjay Krishna, and former Allen School faculty member Yejin Choi, now at Stanford University, also worked on the project. Other collaborators: Mohammadreza Salehi, Jae Sung Park, Vivek Ramanujan and Rohun Tripathi. Henry Wong, second runner-up for the Madrona Prize, with his poster on securing DNA synthesizers. (Photo by Kristine White) The second runner-up , Henry Wong, presented work on securing benchtop DNA synthesizers, machines that let users print synthetic…

articles.title: Apple Says iOS 27.3 Beta Coming Next Week
articles.content: Apple today announced that the first iOS 27.3 developer beta will be released next week and enable some Apple Intelligence features in China . In a press release shared on the Apple Newsroom website in China, Apple said the beta will be released on Wednesday, November 4, but that likely means Tuesday, November 3 in the U.S. due to time zone differences. Apple said iOS 27.3 will then be released to the public in December, but it did not provide a specific date. iOS 27.3 will enable some of the earlier Apple Intelligence features on the iPhone 15 Pro and newer in China, such as Writing Tools, Genmoji, Clean Up, Notification Summaries, Priority Notifications, Visual Intelligence, and Live Translation with AirPods. Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features announced at WWDC 2026 will not be available in China on iOS 27.3, according to Apple. Image Playground will also not be available in China. Apple also said it has partnered with Alibaba to add support for its AI assistant Qwen within Siri, Writing Tools, and Visual Intelligence. Both the iPhone and Siri language will need to be set to English and Chinese (Simplified). Apple Intelligence features will not be available on the Mac, iPad, or other devices in China until Apple receives the necessary approvals, it said. articles.title: Preview web apps live as your coding agent builds them with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime
articles.content: Coding agents now build working web apps: a dashboard, a product page, a prototype that a product team wants to try. The fastest way to review that work is to open the app, use it, ask for a change, and check the result. That loop works well when the app keeps running where the agent edits it, so each change shows up in the browser within seconds. When the app must be copied out and deployed somewhere else first, every change waits for a deployment, and the review slows down to that pace. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with your choice of agent framework and foundation model (FM). AgentCore runtime , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, runs each agent session in its own isolated microVM. With Session endpoints , you can open an app running in that session from your own browser. Session Endpoints give each session an authenticated URL that forwards each request’s HTTP method, path, query string, and body, and WebSocket connections, to the ports you allow. You can watch the page update as the agent saves each file. In this post, you deploy a coding agent that keeps a Vite website running in its session, then open one local page with a chat on the left and the live website on the right. You ask the agent to switch the site to a dark color theme, follow its steps as they stream in, and watch the website change without a refresh. Finally, you look at what happens internally: a second port in the same session, and the requests the Session endpoint refuses. The complete sample, including the notebook this post follows, is in the 14-remote-access folder of the agentcore-samples GitHub repo . How Session endpoints work Each session gets its own Session endpoint, and six details shape how you use it. You choose which ports it reaches. You set allowedPorts when you call CreateAgentRuntime : 1–5 entries, each a single port or a range within 8000–12000, excluding the reserved platform ports . Allowing a port doesn’t start a server, so your application must listen on it, bound to 0.0.0.0 . The URL arrives with the session. The InvokeAgentRuntime response carries it in the X-Amzn-Bedrock-AgentCore-Runtime-Session-Endpoint-Url header, which SDKs that model it expose as sessionEndpointUrl . Every request is authenticated. For a runtime that uses AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) , each HTTP request, HTTP/2 stream, and WebSocket handshake carries a Signature Version 4 (SigV4) signature. The caller also needs bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy on the runtime and its runtime endpoint. For a runtime with an inbound JSON Web Token (JWT) authorizer , each request carries a bearer token instead. Knowing the URL doesn’t grant access. The host name selects the port. Your client connects on port 443 regardless of the target port, and a prefix on the host name chooses the port inside the session: https://8090--<session-endpoint-id>.runtime.bedrock-agentcore.<region>.on.aws/index.html https://8081--<session-endpoint-id>.runtime.bedrock-agentcore.<region>.on.aws/status It carries the protocols your server speaks. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 requests, including server-sent events and gRPC, and WebSocket connections all pass through. This walkthrough uses HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket. It’s scoped to one session. The URL needs credentials on every request and lasts only as long as the session, so use it to build, test, and review what your agent produces. To serve an app to your users, deploy it to a hosting service such as AWS Amplify Hosting . A browser can’t add a SigV4 signature or a bearer token to the requests a page makes on its own, so the Session endpoint client in the bedrock-agentcore SDK can open a local endpoint on your machine. Your browser opens http://localhost:8088 , and the local endpoint adds your credentials to each request and WebSocket handshake before forwarding it. A Session endpoint is different from a runtime endpoint , which AgentCore runtime already provides. Use a…

articles.title: Apple's Flash Storage Suppliers Are Finally 'Getting Their Revenge'
articles.content: The Wall Street Journal 's Rolfe Winkler this week reported that flash storage suppliers once "bullied" by Apple have been "getting their revenge" on the company over the past year due to a severe memory chip shortage, which stems from AI companies building out massive data centers that utilize significant amounts of flash storage and RAM. As the iPhone took off, Apple became the world's largest buyer of flash storage, and naturally that gave the company a lot of leverage in negotiations. The report goes into detail about some of the hardball tactics that were employed by Apple and its former head of procurement, Tony Blevins . "After ordering flash at rock-bottom prices, Apple would refuse delivery at times if flash prices were falling," the report said. "That left suppliers holding piles of unsold chips, including ones custom-made for Apple. Kioxia executives joked they felt like Charlie Brown trying to kick the football—with Lucy always pulling it away." Based in Japan, Kioxia was previously known as the Toshiba Memory Corporation. Apple is also said to have "bullied flash makers into opening their books so it could monitor sales, making sure no one else got a better deal." The report shared another example involving flash storage supplier Sandisk. Apple's other suppliers, such as SK Hynix and Samsung, were not mentioned. "Around the end of 2015, Sandisk refused Apple's requests to send additional supply because it already had customers willing to pay more," the report said. "Blevins threatened a Sandisk salesman with retaliation, saying he would have Sandisk's chief executive, Sanjay Mehrotra, 'crawl on his knees' back to Apple, according to a person familiar with the call." Things changed when the AI era arrived. "Two years ago, Apple bought nearly twice the flash storage of Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Google combined, according to TechInsights estimates," the report said, citing a research firm. "Hyperscalers are now buying double Apple's share." Much of the "revenge" has been passed on to customers, as Apple has raised prices on more than a dozen products this year, including iPhones, iPads, Macs, HomePods, the Apple TV, and more, with the company attributing these increases to the memory chip shortage. Apple's former CEO Tim Cook said price increases were " unavoidable ." Apple is not completely immune, though. Higher prices could result in lower demand, and the report said its profit margins on storage upgrades have been impacted. For example, TechInsights estimated that Apple makes a gross profit of $134 when a customer spends $200 to upgrade an iPhone 18 Pro from 256GB to 512GB of storage, down from $185 when a customer opted for the equivalent upgrade for the iPhone 17 Pro last year. "We've worked with many of our suppliers for decades, and we deeply value their partnership over the years," an Apple spokesperson told The Wall Street Journal . "We look forward to continuing our important work together." On an earnings call this week, SK Hynix forecasted that the memory chip shortage will persist through 2030 , so the pendulum may not swing back in Apple's direction for at least four more years. Eventually, though, it probably will. articles.title: Anthropic VS code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours
articles.content: An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers' machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident. The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont. Both Beaumont and the CTO and co-founder of security firm Phorian said that version 2.1.313 was distributed through Anthropic’s official account on Cursor. So far, neither Cursor nor Anthropic has explained how the attackers gained control of the account. In search of cloud credentials “It was a supply-chain compromise where the attacker gained access to the official distribution channel,” Phorian CTO and co-founder Luke Roberts told Ars. “The malicious version 2.1.313 was posted to the official Anthropic account, effectively superseding 2.1.312. Extensions auto-update in Cursor by default, but users can configure this in settings.” Phorian has more details here . Read full article Comments

articles.title: Sam Altman Thinks Your PC Is Wasting Precious RAM
articles.content: "Looks like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wants to own all the computing resources and rent out terminals to the world as a way of propping up his business plan, now that debt-ridden AI companies are teetering on the edge," writes ancient Slashdot reader Gilmoure. Tom's Hardware reports: In an interview over beers with the YouTube channel Cheeky Pint, Altman said that local inference, and, by extension, people having DRAM in computers at home, is "quite terrible." When discussing local inference on home computers with open-source models, Altman discussed the assumption that people will be able to run local AI on their own computers, the ones they may already own or want to build. Then he explained why that's a bad idea (at the 29-minute mark): "From a global allocation perspective, actually, it's quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5% of the time," Altman said. "You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment. And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that." While OpenAI does have some open-source models, its primary business is in closed-source models that run in data centers, so he's really defending the company's business model. OpenAI isn't exactly threatened by some laptops and gaming rigs just yet, but local AI could mean people one day paying less for subscriptions to models like GPT-6 Luna if they have the power to run them at home. Altman's talk suggests that the company would prefer that more RAM go to OpenAI's data centers rather than home computers, which also sparks enthusiast fears of not being able to own your own hardware or software, but rather rent an agent and a computer in the cloud. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Dartmouth's provost warned us about AI cheating—but his own AI use cost him his job
articles.content: On August 9, 2026, Dartmouth College provost Santiago Schnell wrote a Washington Post op-ed called "Universities are fighting AI cheating. But there’s a deeper problem." This week, Schnell discovered the depths of the problem himself as he resigned from the university after an advisory committee found that he failed to disclose significant AI use in an academic paper and in the Washington Post op-ed, even though publishers required such disclosure. Schnell didn't make it especially easy for the committee to investigate his AI use; the report uses the term "insufficient cooperation." He did turn over his Dartmouth laptop, but he did not turn over logs from his personal LLM accounts related to the writings in question. Nor did he agree to meet with the committee. The committee did get access to the Claude enterprise account Schnell had used through Dartmouth, though. This shows him using the LLM as a tool for revising his papers, finding and fixing bugs in code, and editing or generating figures. articles.title: Darkbloom, which allowed Mac users to rent out their GPUs for AI inference, warns of low payouts
articles.content: Declining token prices have prompted Darkbloom, a distributed inference network, to reassess its business plans. Darkbloom , a project from Seattle-based tech biz Eigen Labs, has developed software that allows anyone with a sufficiently capable macOS device to rent their GPU through the Darkbloom network for interference jobs. In return, they get paid. Through this network, 800 or so participants – including as of two days ago this reporter – have been able to collect a few cents to a few dollars per day by having their hardware handle AI model prompts submitted through OpenRouter , an AI model gateway. In theory, someone running one of Apple's recently released Mac minis with an M5 Pro chip and 64 GB of RAM could earn as much as $192 per month handling incoming inference jobs, per the company's estimate. That assumes full 24/7 utilization during this period on a sought-after model like Qwen3.6 35B A3B, which sells for $0.065/M input tokens, $0.75/M output tokens. But not every network participant has fully surrendered their Mac hardware to the network. The median earnings of the 50 people on the leaderboard amount to about $5.26 per day, $159.86 per month, or $1,918.50 per year. So the best case estimate presented by Darkbloom looks plausible. But it may not be sustainable. The price of tokens – the unit of AI work – has declined, reportedly down 54 percent since May . Ramp's AI Token Price Index , which tracks the price of tokens from Anthropic and OpenAI, shows similar slippage. For Anthropic, the price per million tokens went from $2.65 on May 1, 2026 to $0.62 on October 22, 2026, a decline of 77 percent. In a message shared with Darkbloom participants on the company's Slack channel, Kydo, one of the Eigen Labs researchers working on the distributed inference network, celebrated the network's processing of its trillionth token while attempting to moderate expectations about the project's viability. "Earnings have been low," said Kydo. "For most providers, I don't expect that it is going to recover soon." Pointing to the computational prowess of DeekSeek's DeepInfer framework , he explained that structural changes in the inference market have affected the supply of tokens. "Data centers have become cheaper," he said. "Output per NVIDIA cluster is up ~20x this year, and their margins are wide enough to cut prices 90 percent and still profit at 50 percent." The flood of tokens in turn has washed away the price advantage Darkbloom had previously. "The market caught up to our price," Kydo explained. "We could go lower, but then most of you would earn even less nothing." Finally, he said, the inference routing market is changing, with OpenRouter moving away from price-based routing and putting more emphasis on decode speed, quantization, and prefill speed. For network participants with older or less powerful Mac hardware – those without top of the line Max or Ultra Apple Silicon – "inference won't be worth running," he said. Kydo went on to outline how Darkbloom aims to adapt to the commoditized token market. This involves analyzing model demand to steer participants toward more sought-after models, and looking at ways to provide other kinds of compute work, like distributed CI/CD jobs. For Mac hardware, the focus now appears to be on clusters of high-end Mac Studios (now available with up to 512 GB of RAM), using Apple's Remote Direct Memory Access ( RDMA ) over Thunderbolt. The CI/CD work, based on the observation that AI agents now make pull requests faster than CI/CD pipelines can handle them, will require sandboxing — something the biz expects to begin testing soon. And Darkbloom also aims to improve the performance of its network (in terms of time to first token) and to look for other token buyers beyond OpenRouter. "The next stretch will be a fight, and I expect many machines will leave and Slack will get quieter," Kydo concluded. "But those who stay will be first in line when new earning opportunities come along. We are…

articles.title: The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping
articles.content: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will adopt a new standard that publishers can use to opt out of being scraped by AI, as reported earlier by Search Engine Roundtable . With this control, publishers can apply their AI training preferences across multiple AI companies, instead of setting them individually. The shared "policy token" signal is proposed by Kevin Kelley, a technical lead for standards at Anthropic, as part of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF). articles.title: Over 25% of people lie to get antibiotics—and their lies aren't even good
articles.content: A significant number of patients in the US lie to their doctors to get antibiotics they likely don't need, according to two new studies. While that may not be a startling revelation, the studies drills down on the phenomenon, finding that the lies patients tell are generally bad ones—and yet, they work almost all the time. In the two linked studies published Friday in JAMA Network Open, a team of researchers led by Alistair Thorpe at the University of Utah analyzed online survey data from over 1,000 adults. They found that over a quarter of people reported having lied to a clinician at least once to get an antibiotic prescription for themselves or a child in their care. Patients lied by either exaggerating symptoms, making up symptoms, or—most often—both. But interestingly, the lies people told to get antibiotics involved making up or exaggerating symptoms of infections that wouldn't be treated with antibiotics. For example, the most common falsehoods were symptoms associated with colds, such as fever, cough, and sore throat. That's despite the fact that colds are caused by viruses, not bacteria—which antibiotics treat. Read full article Comments

articles.title: MIT affiliates named 2026 Schmidt Sciences AI2050 Fellows
articles.content: Five MIT faculty members and two additional alumni were recently named to the 2026 cohort of AI2050 Fellows. The honor is announced annually by Schmidt Sciences, Eric and Wendy Schmidt’s philanthropic initiative that aims to accelerate scientific innovation. Conceived and co-chaired by Eric Schmidt and James Manyika, AI2050 is a philanthropic initiative aimed at helping to solve hard problems in artificial intelligence . Within their research, each fellow will contend with the central motivating question of AI2050: “It’s 2050. AI has turned out to be hugely beneficial to society. What happened? What are the most important problems we solved and the opportunities and possibilities we realized to ensure this outcome?” AI2050 Senior Fellow Sendhil Mullainathan is the Peter de Florez Professor at MIT with dual appointments in the departments of Economics and Electrical Engineering and Computer Science who is also a principal investigator at the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. His current research is at the intersection of algorithms and people, with a central focus on launching The Bike Shop@MIT , a new research center that works toward more human-centered AI through scalable bicycles for the mind, and innovative new gears for machine learning algorithms. Mullainathan is the co-founder of ideas42, a nonprofit to apply behavioral science; MIT's Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab, which promotes the use of randomized control trials in development; and Dandelion Health , which combines proprietary AI tools with real-world patient data. He's the co-author of "Scarcity: Why Having Too Little Means So Much." Among other awards, he is a recipient of the MacArthur “Genius Grant”; has been designated a “Young Global Leader” by the World Economic Forum; was labeled a “Top 100 Thinker” by Foreign Policy Magazine; and was named to the “Smart List: 50 people who will change the world” by Wired Magazine (U.K.). He serves on the board of the MacArthur Foundation, is affiliated with the NBER and BREAD, and is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. His AI2050 project focuses on the translation of patterns detectable by AI into testable theories. AI2050 Early Career Fellows Alex Damian is an assistant professor in the Department of Mathematics, holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, who is also a principal investigator at the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. His research focuses on the mathematical foundations of deep learning, with an emphasis on optimization dynamics and representation learning. He was previously a research fellow at the Kempner Institute at Harvard University. He received his PhD in applied and computational mathematics from Princeton University and his BS in mathematics from Duke University. His AI2050 project focuses on effective AI model training. Bailey Flanigan is a Theodore T. Miller (1922) Career Development Assistant Professor at MIT, holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the departments of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and Political Science, and is also a principal investigator at the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. She received her PhD in computer science from Carnegie Mellon University in 2024. In 2024-25, she was a Harvard Data Science Initiative Fellow, hosted at the Harvard Ash Center for Democratic Innovation. Her research combines tools from across disciplines (including social choice theory, game theory, algorithms, statistics, and survey methods) to advance political methodology and strengthen public participation in democracy. She is specifically interested in sampling algorithms, opinion measurement/preference elicitation, and the design of democratic innovations like deliberative minipublics and participatory budgeting. articles.title: Anthropic just removed one of Claude’s biggest usage limits — but not for everyone
articles.content: Claude Code users on Anthropic’s $200 plan will no longer face a rolling five-hour usage cap , provided their accounts are verified and they have weekly usage left. Anthropic announced the change Friday as it renamed its two top consumer plans. Max 5x is now Max, and Max 20x becomes Ultra. They still cost $100 and $200 a month, respectively, and current subscribers don’t need to do anything to switch. Max 5x is now Max, and Max 20x becomes Ultra. Anthropic’s pricing page also lists monthly Claude Platform API credits: $100 with Max and $200 with Ultra. That adds another consideration for developers who use Claude Code while building applications against the API, with each plan bundling API credits equal to its monthly subscription price. Claude Code creator Boris Cherny highlighted the limit change in his own post . What the five-hour cap meant The five-hour limit capped usage within a rolling window, and a demanding task could burn through that allowance much sooner. Claude Code users could hit it midway through debugging or a large refactor and have to wait for a reset despite having weekly usage left. Verification comes first Some Ultra subscribers will have to wait for Anthropic to verify their accounts before the five-hour limit goes away. The company says the checks help prevent fraud and abuse, and it will email users when the cap is lifted. Some Ultra subscribers will have to wait for Anthropic to verify their accounts before the five-hour limit goes away. According to Anthropic’ , verification happens automatically based on account and payment history. There’s no way to request it or speed it up so some users will just have to be patient. The weekly cap remains Ultra users still have the same weekly allowance, and they could use it up sooner without the five-hour limit forcing them to pause. The pricing page lists Ultra at 10 times Pro’s weekly usage, compared with five times Pro’s weekly usage on Max. The pricing page lists Ultra at 10 times Pro’s weekly usage, compared with five times Pro’s weekly usage on Max. Your chats with Claude count toward the same weekly limit as your Claude Code sessions, whether you’re on the web, desktop, or mobile. Once you use up that allowance, you can turn on usage credits to keep working at standard API rates, though you’ll pay extra on top of your subscription. If you keep hitting the session limit with weekly usage to spare, avoiding those interruptions could make Ultra worth the extra $100 a month over Max, but if you already run out before the week is over, removing the session cap won’t give you more included usage. OpenAI eases its limits A day earlier, OpenAI’s Thibault Sottiaux announced higher usage limits for Pro subscribers and Business Premium. OpenAI also dropped a planned cut for existing $200 Pro subscribers after customers objected. In a separate pricing decision, the company abandoned an idea to replace token-based billing with flat per-job fees after developers pushed back. The post Anthropic just removed one of Claude’s biggest usage limits — but not for everyone appeared first on The New Stack .

articles.title: Nvidia store quietly pulls the RTX 5080 following RTX 5090 removal — street prices climb to 2.2X over MSRP
articles.content: First, it was the GeForce RTX 5090 , and now the GeForce RTX 5080 – two of the best graphics cards have gone dark. After the Blackwell flagship left Nvidia's marketplace, the GeForce RTX 5080 followed suit. Prices for the sub-flagship have exploded to more than 2.2X its original $999 MSRP, and the Blackwell-powered graphics card is slowly going out of stock at various U.S. retailers. As with the recent disappearance of the GeForce RTX 5090 on Nvidia’s marketplace, the listings and filters for the GeForce RTX 5080 have also disappeared. While its absence does not necessarily mean Nvidia has discontinued the graphics card, it does raise questions about its status and future availability. This move is especially fishy because other Blackwell SKUs, such as the GeForce RTX 5070 Ti and GeForce RTX 5070 , remain listed on the marketplace, albeit marked as “Out of Stock.” The continued presence of the GeForce RTX 5070 Ti and GeForce RTX 5070 suggests that Nvidia wants to keep the products visible even when they are not immediately available so that consumers can anticipate restocks. The complete removal of the GeForce RTX 5090 and GeForce RTX 5080 breaks that pattern. It fuels rumors that Nvidia has allegedly stopped production of the GeForce RTX 5090 and possibly the GeForce RTX 5080 too, in favor of a rumored GeForce RTX 5080 24GB. (Image credit: Nvidia) Rumors claim Nvidia allegedly stopped producing the GeForce RTX 5090 to repurpose the valuable GB202 silicon into the chipmaker’s RTX Pro Blackwell lineup, which fetches higher margins. This has a lot of credence, since many agree that Nvidia stopped being a gaming hardware vendor long ago and has transformed into an AI provider. Rather than simply discontinuing the GeForce RTX 5090, Nvidia purportedly intends to introduce the GeForce RTX 5080 24GB as the new flagship gaming graphics card. The thing is, a 24GB variant of the GeForce RTX 5080 would solve one of the biggest consumer gripes with the graphics card: the lack of memory. While a GeForce RTX 5080 24GB would offer the same memory as the GeForce RTX 5090, it simply isn't a direct drop-in replacement. The former has 2X fewer CUDA cores, a substantial performance gap that even a 50% memory increase can't make up for. How much money are you willing to spend during the Black Friday sales? The GeForce RTX 5080 launched in January of last year with an MSRP of $999. Demand quickly outpaced supply, and with the rapid price hikes due to the memory shortage, the market price has more than doubled its original MSRP. As of this moment, the most affordable GeForce RTX 5080 in stock, the PNY GeForce RTX 5080 ARGB Epic-X RGB OC, retails for $2,199.99 , which is 2.2X over the original launch price. While some stock remains, it’s selling out fast, and the remaining units will only get more expensive as availability dwindles. At this rate, the GeForce RTX 5080 is unlikely to be available by Black Friday. If you are set on a GeForce RTX 5080, you may have little choice but to act quickly and buy at today's elevated prices. If the GeForce RTX 5080 24GB is indeed legitimate, the graphics card will almost certainly debut at a substantial premium over the original GeForce RTX 5080. Although Nvidia maintains that the RTX 5090 is still alive, the reality suggests otherwise. We have contacted the company for comment regarding the GeForce RTX 5080’s status.

articles.title: Thousands of 'Ghost Students' Use AI to Steal Millions In Student Loans, DOJ Says
articles.content: The Justice Department has charged five people in a crackdown on "ghost student" fraud, in which scammers allegedly use stolen identities and AI to enroll fake students in colleges, complete coursework, and collect federal student loan funds. Ars Technica reports: In a press release Thursday, the Department of Justice said it had uncovered a large-scale scheme relying partly on AI. The DOJ seized more than $750,000 in cryptocurrency from "a network associated with Kenyan nationals" after data analysis helped flag likely fraudsters. Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the DOJ's National Fraud Enforcement Division credited new fraud-detection measures implemented by the Trump administration for the arrests. He said that "this is the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya," while warning fraudsters that the crackdown has only just begun. [...] At a press conference, McDonald was joined by FBI and Department of Education officials to explain how the scheme works. It starts with bad actors purchasing personally identifiable information (PII) of Americans -- most frequently targeting high school graduates who never attended college and went straight into the workforce. Once they have that sensitive data, they fill out the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) while seeking to enroll in universities and community colleges. If accepted, student aid is distributed first to schools to cover tuition and fees, but any leftover money is deposited into bank accounts controlled by the fraudsters. Dozens of Americans have opened bank accounts to act as money mules for fraudsters, the DOJ said. To keep money flowing, bad actors use AI to fill out applications, complete coursework, and even make it appear that a student is attending virtual sessions. "It looks like the ghost student is actually completing the class," McDonald said at the press conference. "Some even create the appearance of a fake student in an online classroom to trick schools into believing a real person is present. The goal is to keep the ghost student in school for as long as possible, semester after semester after semester." So far, the DOE has "identified over 830,000 potentially fraudulent federal student aid accounts created by using this PII of US citizens," officials said at the press conference. If all those accounts are ghost students, total losses come close to $130 million, the DOJ said. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Intel’s woes wipe out $1 trillion of semiconductor market cap in one day — PC market bloodbath leaves few chip stocks unscathed
articles.content: Intel's shares plunged 30% on Friday, wiping out nearly $150 billion in market capitalization in a single day, the largest single-day loss in the company's history. The decline followed a disappointing financial outlook, largely driven by an anticipated drop of more than 20% in sales at Intel's client computing group (CCPG), the company's main cash cow. The declines quickly spread across the semiconductor industry. Although losses elsewhere were nowhere near as severe as Intel's, approximately $1 trillion in semiconductor market capitalization was wiped out on Friday, according to intraday estimates by Benzinga . Fire sale The PHLX Semiconductor Sector Index (SOX), which tracks the stock performance of 30 major semiconductor companies, is one of the key indicators of the industry's financial health. On Friday, the index plunged 9.14%, or 1,052.82 points, to 10,465.38 points as of 2:31 PM ET, as Intel's disappointing outlook triggered a massive selloff across the semiconductor industry. Intel was by far the biggest loser, as other chip-related stocks, while Arm (-12.68%), AMD (-12.48%), Qualcomm (-12.14%), Applied Materials (-8.73%), ASML (-8.13%), Lam Research (-8%), Micron (-7.28%), and Broadcom (-7.1%) suffered considerably less. Then again, while Nvidia lost 5.66% of its market cap, this translates to around $270 billion, which is a massive amount of money. Paradoxically, Nvidia lost more market capitalization in absolute dollar terms than Intel. Go deeper with TH Premium: CPU (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Intel VP Robert Hallock sets Nova Lake expectations, teases return to Raptor Lake for DDR4 platforms CPU scaling with DLSS Intel's one-two punch plan in desktop CPUs is taking shape Benchmarking AMD's BC-250, offering Steam Machine-like performance at half the price AMD splits Zen 7 into three EPYC families for 2028 and starts selling server CPUs by the agent In an unexpected turn of events, the downturn extended to server manufacturers and cloud giants too, as Dell (-12.67%), HPE (-8.10%), Supermicro (-6.96%), and Oracle (-6.88%) lost nearly 7% to 13% of their value. Reuters noted that investors increasingly question the scale of capital investments required to expand AI infrastructure as well as the sustainability of that spending. Gloomy outlook Intel’s client computing and physical AI group (CCPG) generated $8.1 billion in revenue during Q3 2026, down 5% year-over-year and 9% sequentially. Weaker demand and increased competition reduced client processor shipments by 14% year-over-year, which was partially offset by a 9% increase in average selling prices. CCPG accounted for nearly half of Intel's revenue of around $16.5 billion and the company's main source of cash. As strong demand for server processors only partially offsets declining client sales, Intel guided its Q4 revenue to be between $15 billion and $16 billion. Intel expects the client market to deteriorate further in Q4 2026 and into 2027 as elevated memory prices and shortages of other components impact PC prices and demand. In general, Intel expects the client PC market to decline 10% in 2027 compared to 2026, which will inevitably have an effect on CCPG performance. While Intel expects its data center business to continue growing in 2027, industry-wide supply constraints will limit its ability to fully capitalize on demand. 2026 has been a mixed bag for Intel so far. On the one hand, the company achieved its highest market capitalization ever — $673.43 billion in mid-June — on growing sales of data center CPUs, strong sales of client products, and a return to profitability (if the $12.5 billion non-cash accounting charge associated with shares issued to the U.S. government is excluded). On the other hand, the company's capitalization has dropped by nearly 50% to $338.91 billion since mid-June (with $148.68 billion in just one day), as investors began to realize that the performance of Intel's CCPG heavily depends on memory prices, as customers and…

articles.title: iPhone demand sees Apple topple Nvidia as most valuable company, again
articles.content: Tech stocks have been a bloodbath this last week, but Apple's iPhone has supported the company enough with it once more taking the top spot as the most valuable firm in the world. Apple's valuation is down, but the largest in the world That top spot has been going back and forth between Apple and Nvidia for some time now, as iPhone and Services demand go up against AI chip consumption. This time, Apple's stock has been rising on the back of multiple hardware releases, plus the seamless transition of CEO from Tim Cook to John Ternus . Apple stock closed on October 30 down to $344.63, leaving the company with a $5.03 trillion valuation. Nvidia had a tough day too, and finished below AAPL at $204.64 per share, and a $4.93 trillion valuation. This latest valuation comes despite one analyst believing that Apple has confused iPhone buyers. Loop Capital claims that moving the base iPhone launch from September to some point early in 2027 has left buyers unsure. Continue Reading on AppleInsider | Discuss on our Forums
articles.author: William Gallagher <wg@williamgallagher.com>

articles.title: HTTP/3 is faster with some work and help from Cloudflare
articles.content: When you're ordering food from your phone, even time spent navigating the app is time wasted. At the P99 2026 virtual conference , Elvis Chidera , a staff engineer at Germany-based global delivery service Delivery Hero , explained how the company moved most of its user base to HTTP/3, and consequently cut its apps’ total end-to-end response time of the home screen by 17 percent. Chidera, who managed the project, explained that, as promised on the tin, HTTP/3 delivers the web faster than HTTP/2, though it has slow bits that need to be adjusted to work properly. Uber eats Delivery Hero Delivery Hero is all but unknown in the US, which is dominated by Uber Eats and DoorDash. But it is a company with global reach outside the US, with an estimated user base of 60 million across Europe, Latin America, Africa, the Middle East, and Asia. Uber is currently acquiring Delivery Hero for $14.8 billion, with plans to unite the company with Uber Eats. With this purchase, Uber would expand the number of markets where it offers both ride-hailing and delivery services, though not necessarily under the Uber Eats nameplate. Delivery Hero centrally manages separate apps for different regions, all of which it built or acquired. Asians can order poke bowls and sundries through Foodpanda . Turks can order kebabs through Yemeksepeti . Throughout Spain, Italy, Poland, Romania, Ukraine, and much of Africa, the Glovo app is where to ring up the late-night deliveries. And in Latin America, users dial in to PedidosYa to get what they need from nearby farmacias, restaurantes, and mercados. All these regions have widely varying network connectivity, a problem Delivery Hero wanted to minimize. Last mile networking was most often the bottleneck. Apps in Pakistan, for instance, could take nearly a second (at p90) to establish a secure handshake with a server. The engineering team looked at HTTP/3 as a way to lower, even eliminate, that latency. A QUIC-er HTTP The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) formally introduced the third version of the internet’s Hypertext Transfer Protocol in 2022. HTTP is the application layer protocol that connects browsers and other resources connected to servers over the Internet. The previous versions of HTTP were built on the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), which offered guaranteed delivery and flow control. In conjunction with the Internet Protocol (IP), TCP/IP built the modern internet. HTTP/3 replaced TCP with Quick UDP Internet Connection (QUIC), developed by Google , to address some of TCP’s p erceived sluggishness as a transfer protocol. UDP stands for User Datagram Protocol and, unlike TCP, it does not guarantee packet delivery or flow control. UDP is faster because it doesn’t wait around for a signature (QUIC adds in its own flow control on top of UDP). But the UDP-based HTTP/3 reduces, and sometimes eliminates, the round trips needed to secure connections. The app can cache a session ticket and, on a later connection, use QUIC's 0-RTT capability to start sending eligible application data while the handshake is still underway, rather than waiting for it to finish. “Essentially, you can eliminate that one second” of latency that plagued slower networks, Chidera said. “You don't want to pay the cost of two round trips just to exchange data, if you could do it faster.” And unlike HTTP/2, HTTP/3 doesn’t get hung up when packets are lost or delayed. There’s no head-of-line blocking because packets are sent in multiple streams, not just the single string that HTTP/2 offers. Multitask during initialization Setting up HTTP/3 turned out to be surprisingly easy, Chidera found. Delivery Hero used Cloudflare’s content delivery network to serve its global user base, so moving to HTTP/3 involved a simple reconfiguration . Adding HTTP/3 support to the clients, mostly mobile, proved almost as straightforward. Apple has supported HTTP/3 since iOS 15 and most native browsers already support HTTP/3 out of the box. Android proved a…

articles.title: Android Auto can run sideloaded apps for free with this new tool
articles.content: Credit: Andy Walker / Android Authority TL;DR Someone has created a tool called UnknownAuto that lets self-built or sideloaded apps run on Android Auto. The tool marks the app as “installed from Google Play,” so Android Auto accepts it. UnknownAuto is billed as a free, open-source alternative to AA Enabler. Android Auto can run a large variety of apps, but not every app. The platform refuses to run apps that have been sideloaded. If there was ever an app you wished could run on Android Auto but doesn’t, there may be a solution. One user, who goes by u/mannumaster on Reddit, says they wanted to build their own app and use it on Android Auto. When they ran into roadblocks, they created a new tool called UnknownAuto. This tool is free, open-sourced, and can work offline. The creator describes it as an alternative to the proprietary AA Enabler.

articles.title: Busy GPUs can hide slow AI inference on Kubernetes
articles.content: A Kubernetes cluster can be healthy while the AI service running on it disappoints users. A model might return its first token quickly but take too long to finish an answer. It might respond promptly and still give the wrong answer. And a busy GPU tells the operations team little about either outcome. The operational challenge is connecting AI service behavior with the Kubernetes, GPU, compute, storage, and network conditions behind it—not viewing each layer in isolation. That’s why you should measure an inference service before production, then compare live behavior with the baseline. In the fourth article in this HPE-sponsored series on AI and Kubernetes, The New Stack speaks with Marius Bogoevici , Senior Principal Product Manager for HPE Morpheus Software; Mahesh Ramachandran , Vice President of Product Management for HPE OpsRamp Software ; and Karthik Subramanian , Principal Product Manager for HPE Morpheus Software . Inference adds a further question: Does the whole service deliver a useful result at a cost and speed the business can support? Earlier in this series: Part 1: Developers and platform teams both want Kubernetes self-service. They disagree on who owns it. Part 2: A live Kubernetes cluster can still have an ownership gap Part 3: Your Kubernetes dashboard is green. Your users are seeing red. Start with the experience, then establish a baseline For a conversational service, Bogoevici recommends measuring time to first token, time per output token, reliability, capacity, resource efficiency, cost, and answer quality. The right mix depends on the experience a team intends to deliver. A quick first token can mask slow subsequent generation; a fast complete response can still be inaccurate or unhelpful. “A quick first token can mask slow subsequent generation; a fast complete response can still be inaccurate or unhelpful.” Time to first token and time to a complete response answer different questions. Inter-token latency and time per output token help explain generation speed after the first token arrives. Teams should document where they measure each interval and compare results under sustained load and demand spikes. Set targets for the particular workload and user experience. Ramachandran urges teams to profile the AI serving system before customers depend on it. Test representative prompt and context lengths, output volumes, and traffic levels. Record token throughput, latency, and service-level measures under those conditions. The resulting baseline gives operators a reference to measure production behavior changes. Correlating those workload measures with infrastructure performance and capacity helps teams distinguish rising inference demand from resource contention and plan capacity more effectively. As Ramachandran tells The New Stack , teams should “profile it before you launch.” Quality needs its own evaluation. Bogoevici says teams should ask whether the service gives proper answers or hallucinates. Platform telemetry can show a request was served, but data science and domain specialists need representative tests and acceptance criteria for the answer. The newly published ebook, Kubernetes in 2027: Building platforms for AI, autonomy, and scale , recommends assessing output quality alongside service performance and revisiting both after model, prompt, retrieval, or serving changes. When the GPU is busy but the service is slow GPU utilization is a useful signal, but it does not identify the bottleneck . Bogoevici sketches a misleading victory lap: “Our GPUs are maxed at 100%. So we’re doing well.” That tells teams little about how the service actually performs. Ramachandran suggests checking whether inference pods scale on workload-appropriate metrics, whether requests reach the intended model, and whether related components can be scheduled when needed. Different models can have different latency and capacity demands, so a change in request mix can…

articles.title: YouTube bug keeps kicking viewers out of full screen and killing audio
articles.content: TL;DR Some YouTube users are reporting a bug that randomly kicks videos out of full-screen mode and into the floating mini player. The glitch also kills audio playback, forcing users to restart videos or the YouTube app to restore sound. Common troubleshooting steps haven’t helped. We’ve contacted Google to ask whether a fix is in the works. Despite its never-ending battle against ad blockers , YouTube otherwise offers a mostly fuss-free video streaming experience, especially if you’re a Premium subscriber. You open the app, scroll and find something you want to watch, and hit play. But what if even that seamless experience starts showing signs of instability? That’s precisely what some YouTube users, on both Android and iOS, are experiencing right now.

articles.title: Over 300 Chrome extensions found hijacking searches of 13.4 million users — how to stay safe
articles.content: An ongoing security investigation by Socket's John Tuckner (via Bleeping Computer ) has discovered a search-hijacking campaign that involves 319 Chrome extensions with a combined 13.4 million downloads. The malicious extensions redirect search queries through tracking servers to generate advertising revenue from Bing and Yahoo. It's more than double from Tuckner's April report that found "only" 57 Chrome extensions and 6 million downloads. According to Tuckner, the malicious extensions are usually found on websites advertising tools that are labeled as "PDF converter", "AI search", or "safe search". "These extensions were created by a handful of organized operators all working from the same idea: quietly take over the browser's default search engine, route every query through a suspicious proxy server, and collect partner referral payments from Yahoo or Bing under a syndication partner ID," Tuckner wrote. The extensions apparently aren't found on the official Chrome Web Store either. Rather, they're unlisted and are only really found through the shady advertising. How the extensions work (Image credit: Shutterstock) Apparently, the extensions use Chrome's built-in 'chrome_settings_override' setting that lets them replace your default search provider. What this means is that your searches are captured as they pass through the operator's server. After that the redirect could be sent through a site with malware attached, though currently, per Tuckner they're mostly routing to Yahoo and Bing and to falsely claim advertising revenue. "The search referral revenue is a profitable watering hole while the proxy operator can wait for data to accumulate and targets to surface before redirecting to malicious search results or landing pages for phishing or other malicious downloads," Tuckner said. As of this writing, the report says that most of the extensions have been removed the Chrome Web Store when the report was published, however, new ones are constantly being added. "Ultimately, Google can benefit from more advertisements being run and more extensions being listed in the marketplace so there may not be an urgent reason to police this activity too broadly." How to stay safe (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Even if Google isn't policing this specific type of extension, malicious add-ons do slip through to the Chrome Web Store from time to time. When it comes to extensions, you need to be extra careful when downloading and adding them to your browser. Normally, we would recommend you stick to well-known extensions from trusted brands. However, sometimes a lone developer creates one that does exactly what you need. There are several recommendations we have to help you be a bit safer. Check the ratings and reviews of the extensions but also dig into the developer to see if they're legit. Look, even good extensions can go bad , so you want to make sure that your Windows PC is protected with the best antivirus software and that you’re using the best Mac antivirus software on your Apple computer. That way, if an extension is spreading malware or other viruses, they’ll be detected and stopped before they can do any damage. If you're constantly trying different extensions, you should consider one of the best identity theft protection services . They can help get your identity back if it's stolen or recover lost funds due to scams and cyberattacks. articles.title: Dell's 15 touchscreen laptop with 1TB of storage is the office machine I’d recommend to remote workers — especially now it's $300 off at Best Buy
articles.content: In our experience, when it comes to business laptops you can't really go wrong with a Dell. But while the likes of the XPS dominate the high-end, I'm not convinced most professionals need a machine like that. For remote and hybrid workers the Dell 15 laptop for $900 (was $1200) at Best Buy , is an easy pick for productivity that doesn't compromise on power for general office work, emails, video calls, and - of course - streaming movies in your downtime. For me, laptop checks every box and gives you plenty of room for files. • Best for: students, families, and home workers who want a dependable, big-screen everyday laptop with lots of storage. • Why we like it: a 15.3-inch touchscreen with 400 nits of brightness, a generous 1TB SSD, 16GB of memory for smooth multitasking, a backlit keyboard, and a light 3.34-pound design. 15 (Core 7 350): was $1199.99 now $899.99 A 15.3-inch laptop with a 1920 x 1200 IPS touchscreen rated at 400 nits, Intel’s Core 7 350 processor from its new Core Series 3 lineup, integrated Intel graphics, 16GB of memory, a 1TB SSD, a backlit keyboard, HDMI 2.1, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and Windows 11. It weighs 3.34 pounds and comes in Celestial Blue. View Deal Why we recommend it Dell’s mainstream laptops have long been a safe pick for anyone who wants a reliable machine without paying for premium extras, and the 2026 Dell 15 brings a thinner, lighter design and Intel’s new Core Series 3 chips. We haven’t tested it yet, although we've reviewed plenty of similar models from Dell, and have a couple in use at home precisely as WFH machines. The specs are great here, and the 1TB SSD stands out, since most laptops at this price still ship with 512GB. Price Context & Historical Value This is $300, or 25%, off Best Buy’s $1,199.99 comparison price, but since this model just launched, there’s little price history to compare it to. Personally, I think the $1,199.99 list price flatters the discount. Still, $899.99 for 16GB of RAM, 1TB of storage, and a touchscreen is a fair price given how much memory costs have climbed this year. It’s a sensible buy if you need a laptop, but it may well get cheaper as Black Friday nears. Should You Buy It? ✅ Buy the Dell 15 (2026) if... you want a reliable office laptop with a big touchscreen, need plenty of storage for photos and files, or want a light machine that’s easy to carry around the home office, into work, or to class. ❌ Skip the Dell 15 (2026) if... you need a laptop capable of graphics-intensive workloads, as that's beyond what this Dell machine can handle. articles.title: A Claude model autonomously chose a gene therapy and operated on a mouse brain with no human decision-making
articles.content: An AI agent performed brain surgery on an epileptic mouse, picking the drug, the brain target, and the injection coordinates on its own. According to lead researcher Ocana-Santero, it's the first time an AI agent has autonomously chosen a treatment and delivered it to a living mammal. But when a calibration error hit mid-surgery, the agent refused to continue and couldn't be talked out of it. The article A Claude model autonomously chose a gene therapy and operated on a mouse brain with no human decision-making appeared first on The Decoder .

articles.title: 14 New Things Your iPhone Can Do in iOS 27.2
articles.content: Apple released iOS 27.2 on October 26, bringing enhancements to Siri AI, adding Suggestions in Messages, and sneaking in a string of smaller additions across Photos, Podcasts, Games, Apple TV, and FaceTime. iOS 27.2 is available to download to your device now via Settings ➝ General ➝ Software Update. Note that some features may not be available in all regions or on all iPhone models. Apple maintains a feature availability list with all the details. Ask Siri About Past Conversations Siri AI can now recall your past conversations, so you can ask it about something it told you before, like the restaurants it recommended last week. Siri AI features require an iPhone 16 model or later, or an iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 15 Pro Max. Get Answers From More of Your Personal Context Siri AI can now draw from more sources when answering, including photos attached in Messages, Calendar event attendees, and your voicemails. Apple says you'll also get better results from Safari history and Reading List. Use Siri in More Languages Siri AI now supports French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish, in addition to English. Just keep in mind that, as things stand, it's not available in the EU or mainland China. Control Which Apps Siri and Search Can Access A new settings menu has been added that lets you choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access, all from one list. You can find it in Settings ➝ Siri ➝ Excluded Apps. Copy Just Part of a Siri Response Granular text selection lets you select and copy only the part of a Siri response you need, rather than the whole reply. Act on Suggestions in Messages The new Suggestions in Messages feature aims to help you take quick actions based on the context of a conversation, like adding a Calendar invite for a dinner or saving a Reminder. The feature appeared during iOS 27 beta testing but was held back from the initial release , so its arrival has been a good while coming. Manage Shared Albums More Easily Shared Albums in Photos gain three additions. You can now edit captions and comments, the app can avoid adding duplicate photos, and it can display a reminder before an album expires so participants can save important photos and videos. Spot AI-Generated Images iOS 27.2 supports SynthID watermarking, which aims to help you identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground. See What Your Friends Are Playing In the Games app, the Friends tab now provides context around friend suggestions, plus it shows you any recent games your friends have played on their player pages. Create Apple TV Profiles for Your Household If you have an Apple TV, you can now create profiles in the account settings section on iPhone and iPad. All you need for a profile is a name, plus whether it's for an adult or a child. Creating a profile for a child limits content to a PG rating by default, but there's a customize option for finer control. You can select age ratings for TV shows and movies that are appropriate for the child based on their age. Stream FaceTime From Front and Rear Cameras Dual Capture is now available in group ‌FaceTime‌ calls, so you can stream ‌FaceTime‌ video content from the front and rear cameras at the same time. On a compatible device running ‌iOS 27‌.2, flipping the camera while on a ‌FaceTime‌ call automatically turns on Dual Capture. Dual Capture is available on the iPhone 17, ‌iPhone 17‌ Pro, ‌iPhone 17‌ Pro Max, iPhone Air, iPhone 18 Pro, ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ Max, and ‌iPhone Duo‌. Watch Several Live Sports Streams at Once Multiview has been expanded in the Apple TV app to the iPhone, so you can now watch up to four live sports streams at the same time. Multiview works for sports events that come with an ‌Apple TV‌ subscription, so that's Major League Soccer (MLS), Formula 1 (F1) in the U.S., and Friday Night Baseball doubleheaders during the Major League Baseball season. iPhone Duo Edge Light and Apple Pencil Support iOS 27.2 adds Apple…

articles.title: What worries Entire co-founder Thomas Dohmke about the future of tech?
articles.content: Former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke is taking on his old company. His startup, Entire, launched a GitHub alternative this week , replacing traditional pull requests with Trails, a review system that uses AI agents to evaluate code changes while developers oversee the work. A month before that launch, The New Stack asked Dohmke what excites him most about technology’s future and what worries him. He welcomed the ability to turn more of his ideas into working software. His concern was about learning. “What worries me is that people think they no longer need to learn coding,” Entire’s co-founder and CEO told TNS at WeAreDevelopers World Congress North America in San Jose in September. “I think it’s fundamental for every kid out there to not only learn math and biology and geography, but also understand the basics of computer science.” “What worries me is that people think they no longer need to learn coding.” Dohmke was one of several people we posed those questions to at the conference. Their answers reveal enthusiasm for what more people can now build, along with some concerns about understanding, safety, and access to these new tools. For Josh Bentley , SAP’s senior director of community advocacy, broader access to technology means people can build things in hours or days that once took weeks or months. His concern: Whether that speed comes with enough understanding. “People are getting recognized as a builder when they really don’t understand the context of what they’re building,” Bentley said. Darko Mesaroš , distinguished developer advocate at AWS, was similarly excited about more people being able to build software. He also worried about bad code and “AI slop.” “I want people to be able to build more stuff, but I want people to build stuff more intentionally .” “I want people to be able to build more stuff, but I want people to build stuff more intentionally,” Mesaroš said. For Mark Cavage , Docker’s president and chief operating officer, the concern was whether the industry could quickly establish the safeguards and efficiencies needed around AI agents. “The thing that worries me about it, of course, is that actually we as an industry don’t figure out quickly enough how to bring ourselves new efficiencies and trust and safety around it,” Cavage said. Cassidy Williams , GitHub’s senior director of developer advocacy, was excited that people can ask a machine to help turn an idea into something real. She also raised concerns about safety guardrails and the cost of participating. Williams wants people to have accessible tools and “not be priced out from being able to be a part of the future.” The pace of change itself was a source of excitement for Matt Hobbs , head of Cloud, Engineering, Data, and AI at PwC. “Everything that I just built, I could rebuild again and do it better, do it faster, do it safer, do it more ready for enterprise scale,” Hobbs said. Frederic Branczyk , vice president of data engineering at Dash0, described his outlook as cautiously optimistic. He was excited about what AI enables his company to offer customers and how it uses the technology internally, while acknowledging the uncertainty ahead. “None of us really have the answers to all the problems that we’re facing together,” Branczyk said. The conversation is part of The New Stack ’s six-video Inside WeAreDevelopers series. The other five videos explore what developers should learn next, what teams are building, and what brings people together: What should every developer get hands-on with right now? — Speakers make the case for experimenting with GPU programming, local AI models, agent frameworks, and sandboxes. What people missed at WeAreDevelopers — From technical debates to unexpected career connections, attendees explain what…

articles.title: Crim spent $7K+ on AI services in extortion attacks, then left evidence for all to see
articles.content: A n0n ransomware operator tried to break into 23 organizations across 14 countries, but couldn't secure its own front door, leaving its server exposed with all of its methods on view. The criminals used a mix of new (AI) and old (stolen credentials) tooling during their data-theft spree, and in some cases not only stole and encrypted files, but also deleted data and backups, eliminating victims’ ability to recover their information. And despite the fear and hype around the breachpocalypse , with AI finding and developing exploits for critical vulnerabilities affecting most organizations across the globe , these crooks did not exploit a single bug to gain entry into any of their victims’ IT environments. “In every documented compromise in this investigation, access relied on weak or stolen credentials,” said Ensar Seker, chief information security officer of threat intelligence firm SOCRadar. “What stands out is the combination of AI-assisted development and very conventional entry points,” Seker told The Register . “We found no evidence of vulnerability exploitation in the cases examined.” The gang breaks into organizations at scale using widespread Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) scanning and automated FortiGate SSL-VPN credential stuffing. To access US-based IT managed services provider ChiBiTek, the crew used a 15-thread residential SOCKS5 proxy pool to test credentials (ip:port:user:password) against FortiGate portals (GET /remote/login). The operators also gained entry using exposed cloud credentials and reused hosting portal sessions. In one case linked to e-commerce site Fanatics , SOCRadar found that n0n used an exposed AWS access key with permissions to list, read, and delete objects in S3 buckets. The criminals then used this key to pull data from 40 S3 buckets, with up to 110 GB per bucket, and ultimately deleted data, including bank-transaction archives, and purged keys across 12 sensitive buckets. AI-assisted extortion While the threat hunters didn’t find any evidence of a fully autonomous attack system, the ransomware operator did use AI to assist with these intrusions, incurring more than $7,216 in AI usage costs by October 22. Specifically: the criminal or criminals used OpenCode, an open-source AI coding agent, configured with 154 model entries across seven providers. Models included Gemini, Mistral, Nemotron, Llama, Claude, GPT-5.x, Grok, Kimi, GLM, DeepSeek, MiniMax, Qwen, and many, many others, some with safety training removed and others marketed as “uncensored” models. “The operator used AI to write and debug hundreds of scripts. That shows how AI can help an attacker turn basic access into a broader, tailored operation,” Seker said. “The destructive behavior is equally significant,” he added. “The operator did more than steal and encrypt files: in some cases, it deleted data and backups, and in one case changed firewall policies to block traffic. That creates a recovery problem that a decryption key alone cannot solve.” SOCRadar’s threat hunters found the operator’s workspace - a publicly accessible Python HTTP file server hosted in Sweden at 185.157.161[.]148 on port 8877 - last month, and documented the exposed directory in snapshots on September 25 and 26. “Across those snapshots, we identified 1,719 files, including attack scripts, ransomware source code, extortion infrastructure, and an AI coding agent environment,” Seker said. “This gave us visibility into the operation behind the victim listings, including how the operator prepared attacks and handled stolen data.” Meet n0n It also provided a close look at n0n , a newcomer to the data-theft and extortion game that has claimed 108 victims since it emerged last month. On October 12, the group added 38 maritime, port and logistics organizations across 18 countries to its leak site in a single batch. Researchers have linked at least 21 of them to customers of South Korean maritime software provider CyberLogitec, although the software provider has not…

articles.title: This EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic bundle is the home backup battery I’d keep ready for winter storms, and it’s $119 off at Best Buy
articles.content: EcoFlow has been a consistent top-performer in our tests, with one model earning the top spot in our guide to portable power stations. High-capacity, durable build, and reliable output are all strong with this line. So, the EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic with 45W solar panel for $479 (was $598) at Best Buy is an easy recommendation. If a power outage leaves you without heat controls, internet, or a working fridge, the Delta 3 Classic gives you a quiet, fume-free backup you can keep indoors. • Best for: Professionals, campers, and RV owners who want dependable backup power for outages or portable power on the go. • Why we like it: Beyond the strong performance in our tests, this EcoFlow model features 1,024Wh of long-life LFP battery capacity, 1,800W of continuous AC output to run big appliances, 3,000 charge cycles, and a five-year warranty. The solar panels for off-grid use sweeten this one considerably for us. • What you need to know: At $479 it’s good value for the battery alone, though the small panel is more of a bonus for added energy security rather than a serious charging option. Delta 3 Classic: was $598 now $479 A 1,024Wh portable power station with a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery rated for 3,000 cycles, 1,800W of continuous AC output with a 3,600W peak, and a weight of 26.7 pounds. This bundle includes a 45W solar panel and a protective bag, and it comes with a five-year warranty. EcoFlow sells and ships it through Best Buy’s marketplace. View Deal Why We Recommend It EcoFlow is one of the biggest names in portable power, and the Delta 3 Classic is a pared-back version of its Delta 3 that keeps the essentials: a large, long-lasting LFP battery and enough output to run a full-size fridge or a space heater for a while. We haven’t tested this model ourselves, so this pick rests on EcoFlow’s track record and our experience testing other models. Expect fast charging, easy of use, and total dependability if you need additional or on-the-move power supply. The five-year warranty adds welcome peace of mind for a product you may rely on in an emergency. For more top picks, see our guide to the best portable power stations . Price Context & Historical Value This is $119, or 20%, off the bundle’s $598 list price, which is a solid discount on a 1kWh power station with a five-year warranty. Keep in mind that the included 45W panel would take more than a full day of ideal sunlight to refill the battery, so think of it as a top-up tool rather than a full-blown charging solution. If you want backup power in place before winter, this is a good time to buy. Should you buy it? ✅ Buy the EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic bundle if... you want reliable backup power for outages, you need enough output to run a fridge, router, or CPAP machine, or you value a long-life LFP battery with a five-year warranty. ❌ Skip the EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic bundle if... you plan to rely on solar charging, since a 45W panel is far too small to refill this battery quickly, you need a power station that’s easy to carry long distances at 26.7 pounds, or you’d prefer to buy directly from Best Buy rather than a marketplace seller. articles.title: Basically no one is using AI agents for their DoorDash orders
articles.content: As AI tools and agents have continued their march across all aspects of digital life, many companies are trying to use LLMs to improve the experience of purchasing goods and services on the Internet. Thus far, though, a vanishingly small number of people seem to be taking advantage of those capabilities, at least when it comes to using the popular food delivery app DoorDash with an outside AI agent. In a third-quarter earnings call Thursday , DoorDash co-founder and CEO Tony Xu responded to an analyst question by noting that "AI agents are generating several hundred orders [on DoorDash] across the time that they've been up and running." In a marked understatement, Xu called this a "very low use case" for a company that handled just shy of 1 billion orders total in the third quarter of 2026 alone. Speaking generally, Xu said he sees the potential for AI agents to be genuinely helpful for "long consideration purchases" and major decisions where agents would be "doing work on your behalf proactively in the background." However, Xu added, "when it comes to a task that's as simple as ordering food, we tend to see that come directly to DoorDash." Read full article Comments

articles.title: HP's OmniBook X Flip 14 is a surprisingly high-end 2-in-1 touchscreen laptop with a mid-range price in Best Buy's latest sale
articles.content: If you want a laptop that doubles as a tablet for notes, streaming, and sketching without paying premium prices, the OmniBook X Flip delivers a lot for the money. The 2K touchscreen laptop comes equipped with a Core Ultra 5 226V chip that supports up to 40 NPU TOPS for general AI tasks. The 16GB LPDDR5 RAM, and 512GB SSD that makes it ideal for work, study, and downtime. Now, as part of Best Buy's Halloween Doorbuster sale, the HP OmniBook X Flip 14 is $649.99 (was $999.99) . Considering I see sluggish 8GB laptops selling for that price (and I urge you not to buy them), this is an easy recommendation. • Best for: students and professionals who want a stylish, versatile 2-in-1 for work, note-taking, and entertainment. • Why we like it: a sturdy all-metal 2-in-1 design, a high-resolution 14-inch touchscreen, efficient Intel Core Ultra 5 performance with Copilot+ AI features, and battery life that comfortably lasts a workday. OmniBook X Flip 4: was $999.99 now $649.99 A 14-inch 2-in-1 convertible with a 1920 x 1200 IPS touchscreen, an Intel Core Ultra 5 226V processor, 16GB of memory, a 512GB SSD, and Copilot+ PC features, finished in Atmospheric Blue. View Deal Why we recommend it While we haven't reviewed this specification, our sister site Tom’s Guide tested the exact configuration and found it a premium, durable 2-in-1 with a solid display, strong mid-range performance, and more than eight and a half hours of battery life. He did note that it comes loaded with bloatware you’ll want to remove, that the gapless keyboard takes some getting used to, and that the chassis warms up under heavy loads. Those are small trade-offs for a laptop that looks and feels far pricier than it is. Price Context & Historical Value This is $350, or 35%, off the $999.99 list price, but the OmniBook X Flip regularly sells well below that, and Tom’s Guide reviewed it when it was going for $599. That means $649.99 is a good price but not the lowest we’ve seen, and a newer Core Series 3 version is also listed alongside it. Buy now if you need a 2-in-1 today, but it may drop lower over Black Friday next month. Should You Buy It? ✅ Buy the HP OmniBook X Flip 14 if... you want a laptop that converts into a tablet for notes and streaming, you value a sturdy, premium-looking metal design, or you need battery life that lasts a full workday. ❌ Skip the HP OmniBook X Flip 14 if... you’d rather not spend time removing preinstalled bloatware, you prefer a traditional keyboard layout, or you’re willing to wait in case it drops back to $599 for Black Friday. Check out all laptop deals at Best Buy .
