articles.title: Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison thinks AI could make us all rich through a universal high income – but governments will need to change
articles.content: Speaking on-stage at the company's recent AI World conference, Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison declared AI could eventually make everyone "healthier and wealthier". Apparently unfazed by the technology's impacts on humanity, Ellison does acknowledge that governments need to have a shift in mindset to adapt to this new future. In a Q&A during the conference's hotly anticipated final keynote, Ellison outlined a future where AI systems and robots could dramatically reduce the cost of goods and services. But rather than accepting the suggestion that AI would end up replacing us all, he argued that the technology would ultimately serve to make us more productive, allowing workers to achieve things that simply weren't possible before. AI won't replace us, but it will change the economics of work in a lasting way "I think that's kind of nonsensical," Ellison said about predictions that AI will eventually replace everyone. The multi-billionaire accepted AI and automation will inevitably displace some jobs, pointing toward rideshare service s in a hint to ongoing approval of driverless cars in Las Vegas and other cities. But he also stressed not all jobs would be impacted equally, revealing his pilot qualifications on-stage and stressing that autopilot hasn't replaced human pilots despite being a decades-old technology. Although humans will continue to play supervisory roles in many industries (we're already seeing human knowledge worker roles evolve into AI agent managers in some cases), Ellison argued that the overall benefits would be positive, providing governments get involved to support the humans they represent. Painting a picture of what he meant, he described a hypothetical house being constructed entirely by robots in a scenario where automation had replaced human labor. Whereas human labor would have accounted for, say, 80% of the cost of a house before, four-fifths of the house instantly becomes cheaper because of the impact of automation. He used this example to set the foundation for the idea of 'universal high income' – a concept already floated by other tech billionaires, including Elon Musk. Taxation needs to change to enable the provision of a universal income "We need to change from taxing human labor to taxing value added," he said. "So when the robots add value, all that value that the robots add is taxed, and we could have universal high income." Universal high income is an evolution of the universal basic income concept, which provides citizens with a regular payment that covers essential living costs. Instead, he suggested that the enormous productivity gains that AI could eventually unlock could create enough wealth to support much higher incomes, despite declining human work activity. He referenced economist Milton Friedman's negative income tax proposal, describing it as a "reverse income tax" that could help distribute some of the wealth generated by AI. "The robots are adding value. The government's taxing the value... We all become wealthy as a result." However, Ellison's vision is a wildly ambitious one that would require a colossal change to today's systems. It would take more than a decade, he admitted. While a future of AI-induced human wealth with less work might sound far-fetched at best in today's economy, Ellison's optimism remains on track. "All of that is doable," he concluded. layoffs.fyi has tracked over 135,000 layoffs in the tech sector alone in 2026 to date, including around 21,000 Oracle workers in the 12 months between June 2025 and June 2026, and likely thousands more in September 2026 .

articles.title: Mozilla’s plan to rescue us from the zombie internet
articles.content: There is an uneasy feeling these days when surfing the web that the internet has irrevocably changed. Log on to social media and you’re wading through a sea of influencers psy-opping you into buying stuff you don’t need. Scroll through LinkedIn and you can barely tell whether a post was written by a human or generated by Claude to rack up clicks and likes. Everywhere you look, the internet feels a little less human—and increasingly, it is. Recent studies suggest that at least half of the content posted online is AI -generated. How then do we reclaim the internet as a space for genuine human connection and creativity? That’s partly the question the Mozilla Foundation , the 23-year-old accessibility-focused nonprofit behind the Firefox browser, is trying to answer with this year’s MozFest in Barcelona. Held this week, the Mozilla Festival is an annual global gathering of developers, policymakers, and tech builders focused on building a more human future for technology. This year, the festival is asking how to make the internet more human—or, in its words, how to “rewild” it. Fast Company spoke to Nabiha Syed, executive director of the Mozilla Foundation about this year’s festival, its themes, and why she believes nothing about the internet’s future is inevitable. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. Tell me what rewilding means in this context of MozFest? We can acknowledge that we live in a moment where the Internet sometimes feels like a monoculture. There’s like six dudes in hoodies who are making decisions about what everybody should be consuming, the platforms we should be on, the things that shape the market. And what we know from nature is that monoculture works until it doesn’t. Until there’s a collapse in an ecosystem. So much of the open-source ideology that is core to Mozilla is about creating the structures for things to be wild and unpredictable and to go off in different directions and then later cross-pollinate. Last year’s theme for MozFest was unlearning: “Hey, we need to pause. What got us here isn’t necessarily gonna be what gets us to the next place?” Wilding is about saying, “Hey, what would it look like if we just let things bloom?” What if we had more people have more say over the way that we think the internet’s supposed to unfold and be? Describe what was the wild internet? And what is illustrative of a monoculture internet to you? I think about when I first learned how to code it was because I really wanted my MySpace to be amazing. I would view the source and make my page look like whatever I wanted it to look like. When I couldn’t quite get it that way, I’d go to GeoCities and make my own site in my own way. And there was freedom, interoperability, and contestability. Even in the blogosphere, the way that we spoke to one another felt like you were actually having conversations and not worrying about bot interjections. There was a feeling of possibility and not just predetermined ways of interacting like, “You can comment in this way,” or “You can engage in this way.” You got to create and build with the architecture as you wanted it. Every generation is always creative on any communications medium, but within the confines of a platform like Instagram. They can be innovative in how they use Finsta, or the way they shitpost, or the way they talk. But it’s still within the architecture that someone else has designed. What the early internet felt like to me, and to so many people who have nostalgia for that time, is that you could play with the rules of the game, and they were committed to interoperability, transparency, and being able to peer under the hood. Say more about what the consequences of that lack of interoperability, or the confined nature of our current platforms . To me, the big thing is that it creates what we call imagination deficit. articles.title: iPhone Duo Review: One Week Later
articles.content: It's been a week since the iPhone Duo was released, and MacRumors videographer Dan Barbera wanted to revisit his review since he's been able to use the Duo for a longer stretch of time. Subscribe to the MacRumors YouTube channel for more videos. You've probably seen images of iPhone Duos with a bright white line running across one side of the inner display. There is a defect affecting some users, but Apple says it's a problem limited to a small number of units. None of us at MacRumors have had a display crack, and we've seen some AI photos floating around, so it's hard to tell just how many people are actually having problems. iPhone Duos with the hinge issue that causes the display to crack seem to get damaged shortly after purchase, so if you've had an ‌iPhone Duo‌ for the last week and it's still fine, it's not likely to have this defect. The outer display is small, but Dan finds it useful for checking notifications, replying to messages, and scrolling through apps and websites. He unfolds it for multitasking or longer messages, and is a fan of using the ‌iPhone Duo‌ unfolded in portrait mode for watching videos and using an app at the same time. He finds the Touch ID fingerprint sensor easy to find, and says Apple Watch unlock is similar to Face ID . The cameras are just okay, and someone who zooms in a lot is probably going to miss having a telephoto lens. Battery life is between an iPhone 18 Pro and a Pro Max, and for most people, it's likely going to last a full day. Not all apps have been updated for the Duo layout yet, but it's getting better. There's an extension called Wider that extends the Safari window to the edges of the ‌iPhone Duo‌'s outer display, and it's a big improvement. We may see other accommodations in the coming months as developers and users get used to the new layout. Dan says the ‌iPhone Duo‌ is the most excited he's been about an iPhone in a long time, and he plans to keep using it even though he misses having a telephoto lens. Did you get an ‌iPhone Duo‌? What do you think now that you're a week into using it? Let us know in the comments below. articles.title: The Night He Came Home
articles.content: My name is Renan. I lived in Colatina, Brazil. When I was a kid, Halloween did not exist on my street. October arrived hot, with the smell of the Rio Doce in the air and the late afternoon taking its time to go dark. There was no candy at the door, no costumes lined up on the sidewalk. There was, instead, the house we crossed faster, the one someone swore had a story. There were the adults’ warnings: don’t talk to strangers; don’t take long coming back; say where you are. Above all, there was the idea that something could cross the short distance between the gate and the corner and never return a child. In Colatina, “witch” was not a costume imported from an American calendar. It was a word that dropped the volume of a conversation. I still did not know what that meant for real. I only knew that terror did not need a mask to work. Years later, in a dark room, small TV, volume low so the house would not wake up, I reached Halloween , John Carpenter’s 1978 film, for the first time. I don’t remember if it was October. I remember the silence after the final credit. I remember thinking that film, shot in a suburb I had never seen, spoke to a fear I already knew: the quiet street, the half-open door, the “why” that never comes. It felt closer to real dread than any story where the monster explains the monster. Maybe no one can fully explain what makes Halloween so effective. The most we can do, today, is try to understand a few facts. October 31. Or almost. In cinema, Halloween always existed. In American life, too: candy, costumes, the “haunted house” down the street. In Carpenter’s film, the date is not decoration. It is the thesis. The story begins in 1963, on a Halloween night in Haddonfield. A six-year-old boy kills his own sister. Fifteen years later, in 1978, he escapes a psychiatric institution and returns to town. The film does not invent the slasher, but it organizes the genre with an almost cruel clarity: quiet suburb, teenage girl alone, heavy breathing offscreen, and a man, or what is left of a man, reduced to a silhouette. Carpenter and Debra Hill wrote the screenplay in about ten days. The producers had come to him with the idea of a killer who hunted babysitters. There were rumors the original title would be The Babysitter Murders ; Yablans, one of the producers, denied it. The film was always going to take place on Halloween. Carpenter liked that. It seemed too obvious, and for that very reason, no one had fully embraced the date until then. Haddonfield, Illinois, is fiction. The name came from Debra Hill’s hometown in New Jersey. The county on the police badge points to Bowling Green, where Carpenter grew up. Laurie Strode carries the name of an old girlfriend of the director. Michael Myers, that of a British producer. Tommy Doyle and Dr. Samuel Loomis are Hitchcock echoes: Rear Window and Psycho . Jamie Lee Curtis, in her first film, was the daughter of Janet Leigh. American cinema loves those invisible threads. Carpenter did too. The budget was small, somewhere around $325,000. Donald Pleasence, as Loomis, made $20,000. Jamie Lee Curtis, $8,000. Nick Castle, under the mask, $25 a day. The mask came from a costume shop: a William Shatner face, Captain Kirk, bought for less than two dollars, painted white, the eyes widened. The actors’ own clothes, cars rented from a local dealer, dead leaves reused from scene to scene. Shot in spring, in California, with palm trees hidden in the frame and license plates kept out of the way to fake the Midwest. Robert Englund, years before Freddy Krueger, helped scatter leaves to manufacture autumn. The film made tens of millions. But the number matters less than the feeling it left behind: that evil could live in the empty house at the end of the street, the one every child knows, even without knowing the name of whoever died inside. What cannot be explained In real life, after an atrocity, the first question is usually the same: why? The human brain does not tolerate emptiness…

articles.title: US Tech Stocks See Sharp Falls As AI Spending Nears $1 Trillion
articles.content: U.S. technology stocks plunged for a second consecutive day on Friday as investors grew increasingly concerned about the enormous cost of artificial intelligence development and whether those investments will pay off. The Nasdaq fell more than 3.5%, while Intel shares dropped as much as 30%, Reddit fell 26%, and Alphabet extended its losses after shedding more than $500 billion in market value Thursday. The BBC notes that Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon, and Microsoft have collectively committed to spending $800.6 billion on AI in 2026. From the report: Chris Low, from investment management firm FHN Financial, said the bulk of what was happening in the stock market was in reaction to some of the biggest tech players such as Amazon and Google. He told Reuters the companies were "showing some pretty significant growing pains as they aggressively pursue the AI build-out." "The thinking is that these signs suggest that the entire sector is going to slow down." Kathleen Brookes, research director at trading firm XTB, said there have been many ups and downs in AI trade in recent months. "Investors have turned ruthless, punishing any signs of disappointment in [third quarter] earnings," she said. "The AI trade has had a good run in recent years, but now investors want payback, and companies like Alphabet and Intel are in the crosshairs." [...] Brookes noted that November is typically a strong month for stocks. "If we see AI stocks continue to struggle in the coming days, it could suggest the AI trade is past its peak, and investors will be looking for a new theme to drive markets," she said. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Q&A: Hey AI, who should I vote for this year?
articles.content: People are peppering artificial intelligence chatbots everyday with questions, but when it comes to politics and the looming 2026 U.S. midterm elections, what role are AI platforms playing? Could an AI chatbot sway a voter to switch parties or re-examine their political beliefs? MIT researchers have built a new dashboard, called the LLM Election Observatory , to examine, in real-time, how popular AI chatbots are responding to questions about the 2026 midterm elections. The team behind the dashboard — led by Professor Adam Berinsky , Assistant Professor Chara Podimata , and Professor Charles Stewart III — has extensive experience studying voting and election administration, AI and misinformation, and how AI systems are impacting human decision making. In an effort to better understand how AI is shaping the election, they designed the dashboard to simulate how individuals across the country communicate with chatbots. The team tracks how different AI systems respond to the same fixed set of questions on a range of topics, including election certification, hot-button issues, result predictions, news coverage, and more. Every few days, the LLM Election Observatory team runs the questions through the chatbots again, monitoring how their responses vary as the election gets closer depending on user location, political party affiliation, identity and other factors. The goal of this work is not to merely understand how AI systems spread information, but also better comprehend how they are shaping political discourse and voter understanding of political issues across the country. MIT News chatted with Podimata, the Class of 1942 Career Development Professor, an assistant professor of operations research and statistics in the MIT Sloan School of Management, and a member of the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems; and Berinsky, the Mitsui Professor and a professor in the Department of Political Science, about their work with the LLM Election Observatory, how AI could impact the midterms, and what voters should keep in mind when they interact with chatbots. Q : What was the inspiration for this project and what are you hoping to learn through the LLM Election Observatory? Podimata : People are increasingly using AI chatbots to find and make sense of political and election-related information. That makes it important to understand what information these systems actually provide, not just at one moment in time but throughout an election cycle. This is particularly challenging because the models themselves are continually getting updates, the political information inputs available to them are themselves changing, and their answers can depend on how a user asks a question or what information the user provides about themselves. One basic problem is that we currently do not have a good historical record of this information environment. If an AI system gives a particular answer about an election today and gives a different answer several weeks later, it can be very difficult to reconstruct after the fact what voters would have seen at each point in time. One important goal of our project is simply to systematically document that environment as it develops and make the resulting data available to other researchers and to the public. Ultimately, factual accuracy is only the first frontier. We absolutely need to understand whether chatbots provide accurate political information, but we also need to pay just as much attention to the subtler ways in which they may shape people’s understanding of political issues. Differences in framing, emphasis, uncertainty, and cited sources can matter enormously, even in the absence of outright misinformation. What were the main takeaways of that research and how did those findings inform this new project? Podimata : The LLM Election Observatory builds on my previous work during the 2024…

articles.title: MacBook Pro With Touch Display: 15 More Details Revealed
articles.content: Apple on Wednesday unveiled new 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro models with touch-enabled OLED displays , and more details about them continue to be shared by tech reporters who were invited to Apple's hands-on experience in Los Angeles. Nicolas Lellouche of the French website Numerama shared 15 details about the new MacBook Pro models in an article and a social media post . Some of this information has already surfaced, but he provided a useful summary: Apple said the keyboard and trackpad remain the primary input methods, with touch input available as an additional option for those who want it. Apple said there is now a generation of young creators who grew up using touchscreens, so it felt the timing was right to bring the functionality to the Mac. Apple said music creators prefer touch over trackpads for controlling virtual instruments. "Traffic light" controls in the top-left corner of macOS windows expand when pressed. Items in a list become more spaced out when touched. A swipe up from the bottom of the screen brings up the Dock. A swipe down from the top of the screen brings up Spotlight/Siri AI. A long press is equivalent to a right click. Holding a window and quickly moving it left or right triggers Split View. If you close your Mac while your finger is touching the display, touch input is temporarily deactivated to prevent accidental touches. The camera is stabilized so it does not shake on video calls when you touch the screen. You cannot wake the MacBook Pro by touching the screen. Multi-touch supports up to 10 fingers at the same time. No word yet on toes (kidding). Live Activities from iPhone apps can appear in the Dynamic Island. There are settings that allow you to turn off touch input and the illuminated Apple logo on the MacBook Pro's lid. The new MacBook Pro models can be pre-ordered now and launch Friday, November 6. articles.title: I still think the Mac mini M4 is 'the best small form factor PC in the world' — and it’s $150 off at Best Buy
articles.content: The Apple Mac mini M6 may be catching all the headlines right now, but I still think for most people looking for a stylish and powerful mini PC, the Mac mini M4 is the optimal choice. It might lack the extra oomph of the M6, but for daily office tasks and content creation, it's way better value. Case in point. The Apple Mac mini M4 is currently $650 (was $799) at Best Buy . If you want a fast, compact desktop for work, photo editing, or everyday use, and you already own a monitor and keyboard, the Mac mini M4 is the best-value Mac you can buy. Meanwhile, Best Buy has the Mac mini M6 for $799 (was $899) . • Best for: Professionals and creators upgrading an older Mac or Windows mini PC to a powerful, near-silent desktop without paying M6 prices. . • Why we like it: We scored this machine 5 stars in our review, and wondered if it might actually be the best Mac ever. For most people, it will be. Apple’s speedy M4 chip, 16GB of unified memory for smooth multitasking and Apple Intelligence, a tiny five-inch-square design, and handy front-facing USB-C ports and a headphone jack. Mac mini M4: was $799 now $649 A compact desktop with Apple’s M4 chip, 16GB of unified memory, and a 256GB SSD, with front USB-C ports and a headphone jack, plus Thunderbolt, HDMI, and Ethernet on the back. It supports Apple Intelligence and comes in silver. View Deal Why we recommend it In our Mac mini M4 review , our expert Matt awarded it an Editor’s Choice badge and full marks for value, praising its strong performance, much smaller design, and convenient front ports. He called it the cheapest way into the Mac ecosystem, though he noted it struggles with modern games and that its power button sits awkwardly on the underside. Our review unit had a 512GB SSD rather than this model’s 256GB, but it used the same M4 chip and 16GB of memory. Price Context & Historical Value Apple raised the Mac mini’s starting price to $799 earlier this year as memory costs surged, so this $150 discount is measured against Apple’s real current price rather than an inflated list price. It’s still more than the $599 the M4 Mac mini launched at, and well above the sub-$500 deals we saw before the price hike. Given today’s pricing, though, $649 is a strong deal and a good time to buy. articles.title: The Google Nest Wifi Pro is the simplest Wi-Fi 6E mesh router I’d set up for non-techy family members — and it’s half price at Best Buy
articles.content: I don't know about you, but I'm sort of the gadget-man of the family. The tech-head. The makeshift IT consultant that gets called upon whenever there's an issue with technology. If you fall into the same category (or you never want to call on your family IT support again), I'd definitely recommend checking out the Google Nest Wifi Pro 6e Wi-Fi mesh router for $100 (was $200) at Best Buy . The half-price deal makes it incredibly tempting. It's ridiculously simple to set up and manage, making it the ideal no-fuss mesh router pick if you or your family need better connections while working from home. If your home Wi-Fi is spotty and you don’t want to wrestle with complicated router settings, Nest Wifi Pro delivers fast, reliable coverage with minimal setup. • Best for: home workers and families in small to midsize homes needing fast, easy-to-manage Wi-Fi with the option to add more units later. • Why we like it: tri-band Wi-Fi 6E with a 6GHz band for less congestion, up to 2,200 square feet of coverage from one unit, effortless setup through the Google Home app, and support for adding more units to build a mesh. Nest WiFi Pro: was $199 now $99 A single tri-band Wi-Fi 6E (AXE5400) mesh router covering 2.4GHz, 5GHz, and 6GHz bands, with up to 2,200 square feet of coverage, support for up to 100 connected devices, WPA3 security, parental controls, and two Gigabit Ethernet ports. It’s managed through the Google Home app and also works as a Thread border router and Matter controller for smart home devices. Sold by Best Buy. View Deal Why We Recommend It Google built the Nest Wifi Pro for people who want Wi-Fi to simply work, and its app-based setup and automatic updates make it one of the least intimidating routers to own. We haven’t reviewed the Nest Wifi Pro, so this pick rests on Google’s track record with mesh networking and the router’s specs. Its 6GHz band is a real plus if you have newer phones and laptops that support Wi-Fi 6E, since it’s far less crowded than the older bands. Price Context & Historical Value Half off its $199.99 launch price is a strong deal, and $99.99 puts a Wi-Fi 6E mesh router within reach of almost any budget. Keep in mind that it launched in 2022, so it lacks the newer Wi-Fi 7 standard and multi-gig Ethernet found on pricier routers. For most homes with internet plans under 1Gbps, though, it’s a great buy at this price. Should you buy it? ✅ Buy the Google Nest Wifi Pro if... you want fast Wi-Fi that’s easy to set up and manage, your home is under about 2,200 square feet or you plan to add more units, or you use Google Home and want a router that doubles as a smart home hub. ❌ Skip the Google Nest Wifi Pro if... you want Wi-Fi 7 or multi-gig Ethernet ports for a very fast internet plan, you need lots of wired ports, or you already own older Google Wifi or Nest Wifi units, which can’t join a Nest Wifi Pro mesh. articles.title: Filing: Chip startup Powerlattice raises $86M to ease AI’s power crunch
articles.content: Powerlattice founders, from left: Gang Ren, Peng Zou, and Sujith Dermal. (Powerlattice / Walden Kirsch Photo) Powerlattice , a Vancouver, Wash.-based startup developing chips that cut the power demands of AI processors, has raised $86 million, according to an SEC filing on Friday. The new funding is nearly triple the $31 million the company had raised when it emerged from stealth last November with a $25 million Series A led by Playground Global and Celesta Capital. Board members include former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger, a general partner at Playground, and Steve Fu of Celesta. The filing shows Powerlattice is seeking $111 million, with 18 investors participating so far. It does not name the investors or the round. The company declined to comment. AI chips are drawing so much electricity and throwing off so much heat that data center operators are running into limits on available power and cooling. “AI is not constrained by capital, it’s constrained by power,” Gelsinger said last year when Powerlattice announced its Series A. Powerlattice makes what it calls a power delivery chiplet, a small component that sits inside the processor package. Conventional setups route current over long paths to the processor, wasting energy along the way. The company says shortening that path can cut energy use by more than half and boost performance. Powerlattice said last year it was providing engineering samples for GPUs, CPUs and custom accelerators. CEO Peng Zou , Gang Ren and Sujith Dermal founded the company in 2023. The three are semiconductor veterans whose backgrounds span Qualcomm, Intel and NUVIA, a startup Qualcomm acquired in 2021. Powerlattice also has offices in Chandler, Ariz.; San Jose, Calif.; and Hsinchu, Taiwan. Earlier this week, Powerlattice announced it had demonstrated what it calls the industry’s first monolithic integrated voltage regulator chiplet, which packs the controller, power transistors and inductors onto a single piece of silicon. In the test, the chiplet powered a device Powerlattice built to mimic the fast-shifting electrical loads of next-generation AI accelerators. The company says multiple chiplets can be linked to work as one, letting chip designers match the setup to their processors. “Breaking through the AI power wall requires us to rethink how power reaches the processor,” Zou said in the announcement.

articles.title: The Geekom Air12 Lite is the kind of tiny, low-cost PC I’d set up for basic browsing and email — and it’s $269 at Best Buy
articles.content: When it comes to our testing, Geekom has a strong track record in mini PCs. The range runs from high-performance machines for content creation and heavy workloads to compact machines built for general office duty, browsing, streaming, and other undemanding tasks. The Geekom Air12 Lite, currently $269 (was $599) at Best Buy , falls into the latter camp. If you need a small, cheap PC for a kitchen counter, a kid’s homework desk, or a living room TV, the Air12 Lite covers the basics without taking up any space. • Best for: anyone who needs a simple, compact computer for web browsing, email, documents, and streaming video. • Why we like it: a tiny, quiet design, a quad-core Intel N95 processor that handles everyday tasks, a 256GB SSD, and Windows 11 Pro preinstalled. • What you need to know: The Intel N95 is a low-power chip that’s built for browsing, email, office documents, and streaming, but it will feel sluggish with lots of tabs open or more demanding software. Air12 Lite: was $599 now $269 A compact mini PC with a quad-core, four-thread Intel Processor N95 boosting to 3.4GHz, integrated Intel UHD graphics, 8GB of DDR4 memory, a 256GB SSD, and Windows 11 Pro. Sold and shipped by Geekom through Best Buy’s marketplace. View Deal Why we recommend it Geekom has built a solid reputation for well-made mini PCs, and the Air12 Lite is its entry-level model, designed for light everyday tasks rather than heavy workloads. We haven’t tested it ourselves, so this pick rests on Geekom’s track record and the specs. We have, however, tested the improved Air12, which features DDR5 RAM and Wi-Fi 6 connectivity. We scored that machine 4 stars in our review , and for general office tasks, expect performance to be about the same. Price Context & Historical Value Ignore the $599 comparison price, since that’s far more than an N95 mini PC with 8GB of RAM has ever been worth, and budget machines with this chip have typically sold for well under $300. Rising memory prices have pushed up the cost of mini PCs this year, so $269 is a reasonable price today rather than a steal. Buy it if you need a basic PC now, but don’t expect much more than browsing and email from it. Should you buy it? ✅ Buy the Geekom Air12 Lite if... you need an inexpensive, compact PC for browsing, email, documents, and streaming, you want Windows 11 Pro preinstalled, or you’re setting up a simple machine for a family member. ❌ Skip the Geekom Air12 Lite if... you plan to multitask heavily or run demanding apps, since 8GB of RAM and the N95 chip will feel limited; you want to play games; or you’d rather spend a bit more for a mini PC with a faster processor. articles.title: Google’s satellite AI server transmits its first response to Earth
articles.content: Google's AI chip-equipped satellite has generated its first response from space. In a blog post on Friday, Google says it successfully booted up the satellite's Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), allowing the on-board Gemma 4 model to follow through on a prompt to create a haiku about being in space: Blue marble below Data streams in silent grace Starlight feeds my core. ✨ Google says it tried out other space-themed limericks and telemetry prompts as well. The test is part of Google's Project Suncatcher, an experimental initiative that could eventually put AI data centers in space. articles.content: A little over a month ago, we got our first look at Google’s Android-derived line of Googlebooks . Googlebooks are designed to let users seamlessly switch between their phones and laptops to create a true Android ecosystem. It’s a little too early to tell if they’ll succeed, but we wanted to know if they won you over yet. So we asked you which one of the five you would buy (or if you even want one at all) in a poll. The Lenovo Googlebook 15 came out on top with 19% of the vote. It has a 15.3-inch display and comes in at 2.84 pounds, making it the biggest of the group. With Lenovo behind it, it holds the promise of being a reliable, if pricey workhorse, starting at $1,299.

articles.title: The Boulies EP200 is our best-value office chair pick — now the 'archetypal office chair for most people' drops in price in an early Black Friday sale
articles.content: The Boulies EP200 isn't the fanciest office chair to ever pass through our testing grounds. But it is one of the most reliable value picks you can get - far superior. It's been our office furniture editor's daily driver for home-working for since February 2025, and it's as good as the day he got it. It is, he said "the archetypal office chair for most people." Now, as part of the company's early Black Friday sale, the Boulies EP200 is down to $220 (was $310) in the US, while the UK sees the chair discounted to £210 (was £280) . If your home office chair leaves your back aching by mid-afternoon, the Boulies EP200 offers proper ergonomic support without the premium price tag. • Best for: home and office workers who want a comfortable, supportive mesh chair for long days at the desk on a modest budget. • Why we like it: an airy mesh back that keeps you cool, adjustable lumbar support and headrest, adjustable seat depth and armrests, and a sturdy, professional-looking build. EP200: was $309.99 now $219.99 A mesh office chair with adjustable lumbar support, a removable adjustable headrest, four-level seat-depth adjustment, 3D padded armrests, a multi-tilt mechanism with recline up to 120 degrees, a Class 4 gas lift, and a five-star base. It comes in black or green, ships free in the US, and includes a two-year limited warranty and a 14-day return window. UK price: now £210 (was £280) View Deal Why it's worth a look In our Boulies EP200 review , our office furniture editor Steve found it supremely comfortable and breathable, and said he felt no fatigue even after long sessions in it. He also praised its sturdy, stable build and clean, professional look, and his one-year follow-up confirmed it has held up well. His main complaints were that adjustability is more limited than on pricier chairs, which is to be expected, while the mesh back won’t suit anyone who prefers padding. For more picks, including the Boulies EP200, see our guide to the best office chairs . Price & Value Context This is $90, or 29%, off the $309.99 list price. The EP200 dropped to about $200 around the time of our review, so this isn’t a record low, but it’s close. At this price, it’s an easy recommendation for anyone who wants a quality mesh chair without spending $300 or more. articles.title: Rare meteorite from Mars gives us a view into its ancient crust
articles.content: Crater counts tell us that most of the Martian surface is more than 3 billion years old, but pieces of Mars we have on Earth tell a different story. The three main classes of Martian meteorites—shergottites, nakhlites, and chassignites—are all 2.4 billion years old or younger. Until now, only two genuinely ancient Martian meteorites were known: Allan Hills 84001, found in Antarctica, and a jumbled rock from northwest Africa nicknamed Black Beauty. Now we have a third one. A team led by Yang Liu, a planetary scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, has shown that a Martian meteorite called Teghaza 001, found in the Sahara Desert in Mali in 2022, formed at least 4.1 billion years ago. “It's very old and similar to some of the oldest rocks on Earth,” Liu says. A filtered collection “We don't fully understand why old Martian rocks are so rare on Earth," Liu said. Part of the answer may lie in how a piece of Mars gets here. It takes a large impact to launch a rock off the planet, and not every rock can survive that. “If the impact hits into loose powder, it may not get cemented to become a rock and fly off Mars' gravity,” Liu said. “So the natural impact already acts as a filter. Weak rocks do not make it off Mars.” Read full article Comments

articles.content: After being a Google Maps stalwart, I'm now an Apple Maps convert. This is all thanks to a feature that has been a huge help whether I'm traveling longer distances or just heading out for groceries. In short, the "Share ETA" feature allows me to keep other people informed of when I will arrive at my destination. articles.title: GM Reaches $220 Million Settlement Over Selling Drivers' Private Data
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from TechCrunch: General Motors will pay $220 million to 36 states to settle allegations that it illegally sold private driving behavior and location information to data brokers. As part of the settlement, GM must get drivers' express consent before it collects or shares their driving and location data -- terms that are in line with separate agreements it previously reached with California and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC). This settlement does contain a new requirement that GM must have a third party assess the automaker's compliance with the privacy program it has put in place. The agreement announced Thursday settles a lawsuit brought by a coalition of attorneys general from 36 states that alleged GM had sold the information to data brokers, which in turn then sold it to insurance providers. "This agreement addresses Smart Driver, a product we ended in 2024, and reinforces steps we've taken to strengthen our privacy practices," GM said in an emailed statement. "Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it's protected, and the choices customers have about what they share." The settlement comes more than two years after a New York Times report showed how GM and OnStar collected, used, and sold drivers' precise geolocation data and driving behavior to third parties, including data brokers LexisNexis and Verisk. The data was collected through GM's Smart Driver program, a free feature contained within its connected car apps that tracked and rated driving behaviors and seat belt use. Data brokers sold this information to insurance providers, which could affect customers' rates, the NYT reported at the time. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Meet TokenEconomizer: Microsoft’s Plugin That Cuts Coding Agent Costs by Up to 30.9%
articles.content: A team of researchers from Microsoft Research and UC Berkeley have released TokenEconomizer , an open-source cost controller for coding agents. TokenEconomizer is a plugin that learns from past sessions in a repository to cut waste in later ones. It works with Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot CLI and Pi. It does not touch model weights or agent code. On 277 SWE-Bench tasks, it lowered mean cost by 18.4% to 30.9% across 5 agent-model settings. TL;DR Package: A standard-library Python package and agent plugins, with 3 switchable mechanisms. Runs on: Any machine running Claude Code, Codex, Copilot CLI or Pi with Python 3.10+. No GPU and no API key of its own. Performance: 18.4% to 30.9% lower mean SWE-Bench cost, and cheaper in all 30 repository-setting cells. Best: 30.9% lower cost on Claude Code with Opus 4.8 (33.2% when combined with RTK). Worst: Only 6.4% to 9.3% savings on ReposVul audits; Pass@1 drops 1.0 point on Opus 4.8. Why do coding agents waste tokens? Every agent turn re-bills the system prompt, every loaded tool schema and the full history. The research team profiled 60 SWE-Bench tasks across 6 repositories using Claude Code with Opus 4.8. They found 3 recurring sources of waste: Repeated discovery: once 5 tasks precede the current one, 30% of tool calls repeat an earlier action. Unused tools: 23 tool schemas load every turn. 16 are never called, and 3 cover 98% of calls. Failure loops: 10 failed runs were 17% of tasks but 32% of total spend. They also tested 3 fixed open-source strategies: RTK , Serena and Aider’s RepoMap . None was cheaper everywhere. All 3 cut cost on Django and raised it on SymPy. How does TokenEconomizer work? TokenEconomizer is an external controller that treats the agent as a black box. It keeps a state per repository, built from completed traces. Before each task, it sets 3 policies through the prompt, the tool settings and the event stream. 1. Micro-skills An LLM proposer turns trace digests into 1-line facts, such as the working test command. Each fact carries regex detectors that check later traces without a model call. A fact enters the prompt after 3 confirmations on tasks with non-overlapping edited files. Its need rate must also stay at or above 0.4. One contradiction counts as 5 confirmations, so wrong facts retire quickly. 2. Tool pruning Shell, read, write and edit tools are always kept. Other tools are masked after 3 consecutive unused tasks, or when an LLM judge marks them irrelevant. The full catalog returns every 5 tasks for a re-audit. On Django with Claude Code, the first request on task 2 fell from 43,351 to 16,295 prompt tokens. 3. Failure-loop intervention The controller learns a turn budget: 1.25 times the 90th percentile of successful run lengths. Cheap rule checks flag repeated failures or dense errors. An LLM judge then decides if the agent is stuck, at 0.7 confidence or higher. A stuck agent gets 1 redirect, then a stop if the loop recurs. What do the SWE-Bench results show? Setting Cost vs default Pass@1 default Pass@1 TokenEconomizer Claude Code + Sonnet 5 -23.6% 74.7 76.0 Claude Code + Opus 4.8 -30.9% 74.0 73.0 Codex + GPT-5.6 Terra -24.7% 73.8 74.7 Codex + GPT-5.6 Sol -26.1% 80.1 81.7 Copilot CLI + Sonnet 5 -18.4% 75.0 77.6 Source: arXiv 2610.22732 , Table 1. Costs include all controller calls. 3 seeds per setting. Pass@1 improved in 4 of 5 settings. Lower reasoning effort saved cost but cut Pass@1 by 1.8 to 10.3 points. RTK alone raised cost in 12 of 30 repository-setting cells, and RepoMap in 15. Savings build over time. Most repositories cost more at first, but all were cheaper by the sixth task. Alone on Claude Code, tool pruning saved 13.2% to 17.7%, micro-skills 11.8% to 14.3%, and the loop guard 5.4% to 7.1%. Results also held outside SWE-Bench. Costs fell 16.0% to 21.2% on Web-Bench and 16.5% to 19.6% on CredData. ReposVul saw only 6.4% to 9.3%, because shorter runs leave less to remove. How does it compare with other token-saving tools? articles.title: 4 real? Tracking exploitation and patching of eMudhra’s weak keys
articles.content: On October 19, 2026, we learned about eMudhra’s eight shockingly weak keys: where eMudhra was trusted to pick a 115-digit number for their virtual combination lock protecting the Internet, they picked the number 4. Not even four digits, just the number 4. The other seven keys were similarly weak: 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237. The next day, we wrote a blog post on the immediate action we took to mitigate this leak, and what customers needed to do on their end to stay secure. Now, we are sharing a more in-depth follow up on the evidence we’ve seen of exploitation, and the progress seen on visitors patching their systems. Let's start with the scale of the problem. A certificate authority (CA) with weak keys this serious is unprecedented, and the potential consequences are significant. While there have been plenty of compromised certification authorities in the past (such as DigiNotar , TÜRKTRUST , and TrustWave ), access to their keys has always been contained to a degree; these incidents gave a limited set of attackers or organizations the ability to issue fraudulent certificates. The eMudhra incident is fundamentally different; the affected intermediate private keys could be recovered almost instantly by anyone from the public certificates themselves. Anyone can independently recover these same signing keys and create certificates for any domain that an unpatched client not enforcing Certificate Transparency would accept. eMudhra announced they’re exiting the public CA business and have claimed a mistake in a key generation script, but have not yet shared the script. They signed a certificate revocation list (CRL) with what might’ve been a correctly generated key, and subsequently corrected it to be signed with the weak key. How did that come to be and why didn’t that set off alarms? Much has to be cleared up, including the role of the auditors and cross signers. This blog proposes the fixes and next steps for organizations to ensure they are secure. Patching Cloudflare Our primary concern remains the security impact on Cloudflare, our customers, and the Internet as a whole. At the time of writing, all high priority Cloudflare systems have been patched. A small number of confirmed low impact tickets is being worked on. We started patching high-impact systems immediately on October 19. These included customer origin-facing proxies using Pingora , responsible for most of our outbound connections. These were patched in hours to reject the vulnerable eMudhra keys. At the same time, we started an AI-assisted analysis of our source code to find all other systems that trust these weak keys. Within four hours we had a full analysis. We assigned a ticket with preliminary analysis for each system, and asked the team to confirm and/or adjust the analysis before the end of the day. Where high impact was identified, we asked to patch immediately, and for the lower impact, remediation was due at the end of last week. Has Cloudflare seen exploitation across its network? To track whenever a customer’s server (or attacker) presents a certificate signed by eMudhra’s weak keys, we added logging to Pingora. As this outbound service accounts for the vast majority of outgoing TLS connections from a Cloudflare machine, any attacker attempting to snoop using the eMudhra keys would trigger this logging. The logging finished rolling out October 21. At the time of writing, a week later, we’ve seen about 22,000 attempted handshakes with the weak eMudhra keys. Two-thirds of the attempts were fetches of test sites such as emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com (which we mentioned in the developer guidance in our earlier post). Almost all of the remaining third went to origins who appeared to set up a certificate for themselves using the weak intermediate. Every handshake configured to verify the certificate was refused, as we already patched. About 160 of these handshakes stood out: the certificates’ Subject Alternative Names (SANs) were naming other…

articles.title: Fujifilm to boost tape production 5x as AI fuels archiving demand
articles.content: In an announcement released Thursday, Fujifilm said it will invest roughly 10 billion yen (about $63 million) to increase its production capacity fivefold for an unlikely beneficiary of the AI era: magnetic tape. Fujifilm attributes the surge in archiving demand to the spread of generative AI, which the company remarked is producing "exponential growth" in data needs worldwide. The 5x increase in production capacity will be measured against fiscal year 2025 production levels. The investment in Fujifilm's Kanagawa Factory, Odawara site will make it "the largest investment Fujifilm has made to date in dedicated LTO tape facilities." The project will run from fiscal years 2026 through 2028 to fund manufacturing expansion and additional personnel, primarily to produce the latest-generation "FUJIFILM LTO Ultrium10" tape. articles.title: AI Security Agents Compared: Claude, Codex, Mantis, Cloudflare
articles.content: Anthropic, OpenAI, Cloudflare and Google now each ship an AI agent that hunts security bugs in source code. We checked the repos, docs and technical details behind each one. The key finding: all 4 tools converge on one design. One agent finds a bug, a separate agent tries to disprove it, and only survivors get a patch. The differences are in where they run, who can use them and how much proof they demand. Key Takeaways 4 labs, 1 pattern: find, independently disprove, then patch. Claude Security runs inside Claude Code; no extra API key needed. Codex Security’s CLI is Apache-2.0, but scanning still needs OpenAI access. Cloudflare’s skill is MIT, model-agnostic and the most-starred at 47.5K. Google’s Mantis reproduces bugs in a sandbox; Google says isolate it. Why 4 labs shipped the same thing in 2026 The problem every one of them is solving is noise. Google’s security team writes that sloppy AI code scanning produces hallucinated bugs and true-positive rates under 7% . A scanner that is wrong 93% of the time costs reviewers more than it saves. The shared fix is separation of duties. The agent that reports a finding never gets to confirm it. Cloudflare states the rule directly in its README: the verifier is never the agent that found the bug. Anthropic, OpenAI and Google each describe a similar validation step before anything reaches a report. The second driver is offense. Anthropic team states that it built its scanner partly because attackers were already using AI models to find exploitable flaws, per The Hacker News . Google opens its Mantis post by noting that models can now discover and exploit bugs with little human help. 1. Claude Security by Anthropic What it is: A multi-agent vulnerability scanner that runs inside a Claude Code session. It is the local version of Anthropic’s hosted Claude Security product, per the plugin README . How it works: Agents map the architecture, build a threat model, hunt across every component and verify each finding independently. The plugin offers 3 jobs from one menu: scan the codebase, scan changes, or suggest patches, per Claude Code docs . Output: A Markdown report along with a SARIF 2.1.0 file for GitHub code scanning. Each finding carries severity, a CWE category, impact and reproduction steps. Patches are drafted in a scratch copy and land as F<n>.patch files. The plugin never commits, pushes or opens a pull request on its own. Cost and access: It makes no model calls of its own, so there is no separate API key. Scans count against your Claude plan’s usage limits. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser /plugin install claude-security@claude-plugins-official /claude-security Timeline: Anthropic opened a limited preview called Claude Code Security in February 2026. The hosted product reached public beta for Enterprise customers on Claude Opus 4.7 . The Claude Code plugin entered beta on July 22, 2026, per Cybersecurity News . In August, the hosted scanner moved to Claude Mythos 5, per Dataconomy . Where it fits: Anthropic positions it as one layer. The security-guidance plugin checks code as Claude writes it, and /security-review does a single pass on a branch. Claude Security is the on-demand deep scan. 2. Codex Security by OpenAI What it is: A CLI and TypeScript SDK, published as @openai/codex-security, for finding, validating and fixing vulnerabilities. How it works: It scans a whole repo, selected paths, or a Git diff. A –mode deep flag runs parallel discovery workers. It validates candidate findings, generates patches and can verify existing fixes. A cs policy command drafts a SECURITY.md that tells future scans what counts as a vulnerability in your project. Output: Threat models, SARIF, JSON or CSV exports, plus publishing to Linear. It can import GitHub code-scanning alerts and suggest owners from Git history. A GitHub Action runs scheduled or pull-request scans; findings are report-only by default. Copy Code Copied Use a different…

articles.title: How Worldwide Express automated freight exceptions with Amazon Bedrock
articles.content: Worldwide Express (part of ShipStation Global) had built something big: approximately $5 billion in systemwide revenue, over 75 less-than-truckload (LTL) carriers and more than 130,000 customers. But that same scale had a hidden cost. Every month, $15 million in free cash flow sat frozen, locked in billing exceptions no one had resolved yet. Each one had to be chased down by hand, carrier by carrier, with its own rules to check. Worldwide Express outsourced to a team that worked cases one at a time, calling customers and carriers for each dispute. The exceptions piled up, cash stayed stuck, and every order took longer to turn into money. Worldwide Express worked with AWS and LTM to build a multi-agentic AI solution with Amazon Bedrock that plugs directly into their transportation management system (TMS), SpeedShip. Six months after launch, the company reported a 75 percent reduction in active exceptions, a 4-week improvement in time-to-cash, $1M annual savings, and a one-time $10M free cash flow infusion. In this post, we describe the challenge, explain how Worldwide Express designed the multi-agent solution, and share the results. The challenge In LTL freight, roughly 14 percent of invoices fail the standard three-way match between the purchase order, the goods receipt, and the carrier invoice. When a match fails, the invoice enters exception handling. For Worldwide Express, exceptions fell into three categories: Line-item mismatches: Quantities or service codes that didn’t align with the shipment record. Pricing variances: The carrier billed a rate different from the contracted price. Unexpected accessorial charges: Liftgate fees, residential surcharges, or reweigh adjustments that weren’t on the original quote. Each exception triggered a five-step manual process: Identify the exception type by cross-referencing the invoice against the purchase order, goods receipt, and pricing. Research the root cause in vendor records. Send email to the carrier or warehouse with dispute details. Wait for a response. Execute the resolution in the TMS. With each carrier operating under its own tariff structure and dispute workflow, this process consumed most of the FinOps team’s bandwidth. Rule-based process automation (RPA) can handle structured, predictable workflows. However, exception resolution requires contextual judgment: interpreting a carrier’s accessorial policy, comparing charges against shipment data, and deciding validity given a carrier, exception type, and dollar amount. That variability is what made the problem a fit for the agentic AI framework. From assessment to production In June 2025, Worldwide Express engaged the AWS Business Transformation & Value Advisory team to identify 19 automation opportunities across the Order-to-Cash lifecycle. Knowing the business value of exceptions automation, Worldwide Express moved from assessment to production in less than 6 months. How it works The solution runs on AWS. Amazon Bedrock provides AI reasoning, and Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) is the engine. The design calls for fine-grained control over how each agent reasons, where decision boundaries sit, and how exceptions are routed between agents. Building the framework directly on Amazon EC2, with Amazon Bedrock providing inference, keeps that orchestration logic fully in the team’s hands and supports open source agent libraries. Production controls of business logic make each agent’s role, inputs, and decision boundaries explicit and auditable. In a billing-dispute workflow, every automated decision needs to be explainable. Agents When an invoice exception is detected, the system routes it to one of three specialized AI agents, each handling a specific type of billing dispute: Invoice Matching Agent finds the matching shipment record and flags what doesn’t line up. Pricing Variance Agent compares the carrier’s charge against the contracted rate and determines whether the difference is valid. Accessorial Validation Agent…

articles.title: The company behind ‘PUBG’ wants to bring video game AI into the real world
articles.content: The robotics industry wants humanoids to become part of everyday life, taking on work in homes and offices. Billions of dollars are flowing toward machines capable of increasingly complex physical tasks. The humanoid robot maker Figure raised more than $1 billion last year at a $39 billion valuation, while the robotics software startup Skild AI secured $1.4 billion in January to develop artificial intelligence that can control different kinds of robots. But working alongside people requires understanding incomplete instructions and adapting when someone changes their mind midway through a task. A robot that needs constant explanations could leave its owner supervising the very work they hoped to hand over. Krafton believes its video game experience could help solve that problem. The South Korean developer behind PUBG: Battlegrounds has spent nearly two decades creating virtual worlds where software responds to unpredictable player decisions. Its Palo Alto subsidiary, Ludo Robotics, is now applying that expertise to AI that helps robots understand human requests and decide how to act. CH Kim, CEO of both companies, sees Krafton’s experience developing AI teammates as a starting point. Developed with the chipmaker Nvidia, PUBG Ally is what the companies describe as “the world’s first voice-enabled coplayable character (CPC),” an AI teammate that goes beyond traditional nonplayable characters (NPCs) by cooperating with players, adapting to gameplay and remembering previous interactions. Ludo Robotics hopes to bring those capabilities into the physical world. “We’ve been developing AI in the form of nonplayer characters, or NPCs, for our video games even before the recent wave of interest in the [AI] sector. With the latest large language models and AI technologies, we’ve been able to give our in-game NPCs greater intelligence,” Kim tells Fast Company . “We reached a point where we started thinking about what would happen if we brought these AI characters out of virtual worlds and into the real world. That’s essentially physical AI, and that’s how we came to work on Ludi.” Ludo Robotics is set to present Ludi 0.2, its latest experimental robotic intelligence system, at the Bay Area Robotics Symposium at the University of California, Berkeley. The new version aims to improve conversational memory and gesture recognition, though Kim acknowledges that Ludi remains a research demonstration, not yet reliable enough for everyday use. The gaming news outlet Inven Global, citing Krafton’s PUBG Ally report , put combat performance at 2.58 out of 5. Half of respondents viewed the character as a tool, while just 18.5% considered her a teammate. CH Kim [Photo: Krafton] “The foundational technology we’ve applied to PUBG Ally is very similar to the technology we’re applying to Ludi,” Kim explained. “We’re building on those capabilities as we move forward, and our longer-term goal is to expand this work into developing our own proprietary foundation model.” Krafton believes its gaming expertise offers a competitive advantage in humanoid robotics. articles.title: Hackers hijacked a Claude Code extension, exposing yet another new AI security risk
articles.content: The world can feel particularly unsafe these days, with AI agents running rampant within private networks and billions of dollars disappearing from crypto wallets in less time than it takes to watch a sitcom episode. But while the world was watching Binance’s massive crypto heist , another potentially consequential security breach was unfolding largely under the radar. For roughly 11 hours, a malicious version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension was available on Cursor’s VS Code extension marketplace. The extension—which allows developers to use Anthropic’s AI coding assistant within Cursor to write, edit, and debug software—had been tampered with to collect information about users’ computers and attempt to install a persistent backdoor. That backdoor used Secure Shell (SSH), a tool for remotely accessing computers, and could potentially have allowed hackers to access victims’ machines even after the extension was removed. Cursor disclosed the breach in a blog post , saying it removed the compromised extension as soon as it discovered the problem. The company also emphasized that the mechanism intended to give hackers remote access was unlikely to have worked in many cases because of flaws in its code. Anthropic, meanwhile, said in a statement that the incident “only impacts Cursor users” and was unrelated to Anthropic’s own systems. According to Cursor’s security notice , the malicious extension was designed to leave behind scripts that would attempt to reconnect to the hackers’ server every minute, even after the extension had been removed. Cursor says it has since worked with the server’s hosting provider to take the server offline and to temporarily shut down and rebuild its extension marketplace. The company found no evidence that other extensions were compromised. Still, it is urging anyone who installed the affected version on October 29 to check their computers for signs of infection, remove any unauthorized access, and consider changing potentially compromised credentials. The hackers’ identities remain unknown, but security experts say the incident illustrates an increasingly troubling risk as AI coding tools become embedded in developers’ workflows. “The scenario of Claude sending out poisoned agents everywhere makes me even more worried than I already was,” says Eerke Boiten, a professor of cybersecurity at De Montfort University in England. Gwen van der Velden, a professor of education at the University of Warwick who’s working on a program to help rebuild Ukraine, says the choice of the Claude Code extension is particularly “interesting” given the potential for such tools to be exploited in hybrid warfare. “We know from the Russian side, it is of great interest to them,” she says. “If you were to go for hybrid warfare, where you use this kind of technology, then actually getting 5,000 bits of malware reproducing itself through AI agents is a powerful thing.” The broader concern isn’t simply that a malicious extension could compromise individual computers. It’s that the growing ecosystem of AI coding assistants and their associated tools is creating new pathways into sensitive systems. “This is a classic example of how everyone has been focussing on LLMs attacking other systems, yet forgetting about the fact that LLMs and their associated tools are increasing the attack surface across some very sensitive IT estates,” says Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at the University of Surrey. And even a relatively limited breach could carry outsized consequences when the targets are software developers with access to sensitive code and infrastructure. “While 5,000 users might sound relatively small, these are developers who have access to highly sensitive systems and source code, so the potential impact will be far greater than the numbers suggest,” says Jake Moore, a threat adviser with the global cybersecurity firm ESET. “Software extensions have eased…

articles.title: Kubernetes just formed a workload conformance group. Here’s why it matters for AI teams.
articles.content: Welcome to the final edition of Road to KubeCon , where we track the Kubernetes and cloud-native ecosystem each week on The New Stack as we head into KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, November 9-12 in Salt Lake City, Utah. This week we explore how Kubernetes is getting new guidance for running AI workloads, including a new book from TNS, a dedicated Kubernetes working group, and advice on running LLMs across multiple GPUs. Also in this day-before-Halloween-timed column, we’ve got OTel operators speaking a new language, security horrors from the latest AGNTCon + MCPCon, and untangling the dark webs of Kubernetes pod troubleshooting gone awry. Join the conversation with HPE at KubeCon HPE will have a big presence at KubeCon NA this year. The gold sponsor will be at Booths 151 and 145, where they’ll present live sessions throughout the day on topics spanning vSphere, HPE Kubernetes Service (HKS), distributed inference, setting up cloud storage for Kubernetes, and more. Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) is a presenting sponsor of Road to KubeCon. HPE Software helps IT organizations modernize infrastructure, streamline operations, and accelerate AI initiatives across hybrid, multi-vendor environments. This year, the focus is on gaining visibility and control across Kubernetes environments across VMs, infrastructure, and clouds. If you’d like to schedule a meeting with an HPE representative, contact jennifer.osuna@hpe.com. TNS publishes Kubernetes guidebook for 2027 In partnership with HPE, The New Stack has published a helpful book containing ten checks for teams running AI workloads on Kubernetes. The book, Kubernetes in 2027: Building Platforms for AI, Autonomy, and Scale , is available for download now. Written by contributing writer Chris J. Preimesberger , the guide spans the full lifecycle, covering how to stress-test infrastructure before launch, how to meet the nuanced demands of agentic AI, what to watch for, and how to develop stronger permissioning models for agents. Since agentic AI is prone to bursty, unpredictable behavior, arming your infrastructure with the right approach on Kubernetes is an important first step to production stability and success with AI at scale. Kubernetes gets a Workload Conformance Working Group Workload types have been expanding for years. And AI undoubtedly adds more variety. Against this backdrop, on Tuesday, October 27, the Kubernetes community announced a dedicated Workload Conformance Working Group . According to Broadcom’s Nabarun Pal , writing on behalf of WG Workload Conformance on the Kubernetes blog , “The working group is writing a shared standard for how workloads behave at runtime on Kubernetes.” To do so, they’ll need community input, Pal adds. The Kubernetes AI Conformance test already determines whether a cluster can run AI or machine learning (ML) workloads. Yet none currently exists for workloads, requiring workarounds, manual exploration, or monitoring for signs like node drain or permission issues. So the new WG aims to create a similar standard for workloads. It’s a significant step forward as the Kubernetes community grapples with a growing variety of workloads, including AI. Interested parties can read the working group proposal for more information, join the Slack channel , or attend biweekly meetings to get involved. OpenTelemetry Transformation Language reaches v1 Earlier this week, the OpenTelemetry (OTel) project reached a milestone: the OpenTelemetry Transformation Language (OTTL) has reached v1 . It’s stable for traces, metrics, and logs, and is included within Collector Contrib v0.164.0 and onward. As Grafana Labs’ Tyler Helmuth recounts on the OTel blog , OTTL was created in 2022 as the configuration language for the transform processor. The domain-specific language lets you modify, filter, and enrich telemetry data directly at the collector level. Longevity-thinkers will like this: They’ve also made a…

articles.title: Configure the ChatGPT desktop app with Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US)
articles.content: The ChatGPT desktop app is now available on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US) , providing access to OpenAI’s frontier models through two components. Work completes complex, multi-step tasks and delivers review-ready results, and Codex is a coding agent for developing, testing, and reviewing software. This walkthrough is intended for organizations whose security architecture requires model inference to use AWS GovCloud (US) identities, endpoints, and Regional controls. It configures Codex to route model requests through Amazon Bedrock Mantle in us-gov-west-1 , where access can be governed using AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and existing AWS GovCloud (US) network controls. Codex is the OpenAI coding agent for AI-powered software development. With GPT models powering inference, Codex introduces a new class of intelligence optimized for complex, long-horizon developer workflows. You can use the ChatGPT desktop app, the Codex CLI, and IDE integrations with Visual Studio Code, JetBrains, and Xcode. Model inference is routed through the Responses API on Amazon Bedrock. For customers with data residency requirements, processing stays within the Amazon Bedrock AWS Region that you select. You pay per token with no seat licenses and no per-developer commitments. Zero data retention (ZDR) is also supported. In this configurable mode, prompts and responses are processed without being written to durable storage by AWS or shared with model providers. This helps you protect sensitive information and meet stringent data-governance, privacy, and security requirements. This post walks through a controlled local deployment of the ChatGPT desktop app that sends model inference to Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US-West). The configuration uses API-mode sign-in, a managed device policy, a named AWS profile, and network restrictions. These restrictions allow access only to the approved Amazon Bedrock endpoint while disabling other external connections and network-enabled capabilities. The result is a deployment that an agency security team can test and document before approving broader use. Using AWS GovCloud (US) and following this guide do not, by themselves, authorize your workload. Your organization remains responsible for reviewing the selected model, AWS services, Region, endpoint, workstation controls, repositories, credentials, and data flows against its system security plan and authorization process. Solution overview You can use the ChatGPT desktop app in two ways: Work for larger tasks that need planning, research, files, and a finished result. Codex for technical work such as editing code, running tests, and reviewing pull requests. The ChatGPT desktop app runs on an organization-managed computer through the desktop app or CLI. It uses the configured AWS credentials to securely send requests to the Amazon Bedrock Mantle endpoint in us-gov-west-1 . Because this setup uses AWS directly, ChatGPT workspace rules and user roles don’t control it. The main security controls are the computer’s policies and the AWS identity and permissions being used. Walkthrough The configuration has three main steps: set up authentication, set up the ChatGPT desktop app configuration files, and then launch, initialize, and verify the deployment. Prerequisites Before setting up the ChatGPT desktop app with AWS GovCloud (US), make sure your version of the ChatGPT desktop app supports Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US). You need an approved AWS GovCloud (US) account, an IAM identity and approved credentials, access to the approved model, AWS Region, and endpoint, and permission to use them. You also need to set up the requirements.toml and config.toml files. Step 1: Set up authentication Select the approved AWS GovCloud (US) account and IAM identity or role with access to the approved model in us-gov-west-1 . articles.title: Metal fabricator NIC Global to cut 103 jobs near Seattle, move production to Eastern Washington
articles.content: NIC Global is closing its 100,000-square-foot manufacturing site in Woodinville, Wash., as demand shifts to Eastern Washington. (NIC Photo) Metal fabricator NIC Global plans to close its Woodinville, Wash., plant, eliminating 103 jobs. Declining business from local customers is prompting the company to shift production primarily to Eastern Washington to meet data center-related growth. The layoffs are scheduled to begin Jan. 18, 2027, with final departures Aug. 31, 2028, according to a notice filed with the Washington Employment Security Department. Affected jobs include assembly, engineering, quality assurance, metal fabrication specialists, and forklift positions. The building will be returned to its landlord when the lease ends in September 2028. “This is a sad day for our company. Woodinville is where NIC was formed — three Seattle-area sheet-metal shops brought together under one roof in 2001 — and the people in that building built the foundation of everything NIC is today,” Troy Wood, company president and CEO, said via email. The 100,000-square-foot site mostly served energy and medical device customers. Wood said the volume of work at the plant has declined while demand has increased in Eastern Washington for customers building power distribution technology needed by data centers. “NIC is a supplier of sheet-metal fabrications and assemblies, and in our business, being close to our customers is what keeps us competitive,” Wood said. While most of the work from Woodinville will go to Spokane, and a smaller portion will go to NIC’s Gallatin, Tenn., facility. The company also has manufacturing in Pullman; Chillicothe, Ohio; and Denton, Texas. The work outside of Washington is focused on the heavy truck sector. The company’s headcount is nearly 600. Laid-off workers will be encouraged to apply for openings at other plants. There are smaller fabricators remaining in the Seattle area, including JEMCO Components & Fabrications, which provides precision machining and sheet-metal fabrication for customers in medical, aerospace and defense sectors, and QUAL-FAB serving medical and dental customers. NIC’s legal and financial headquarters will stay in the Woodinville area, where the company plans a new office for its finance, IT, sales and West Coast support teams. Wood praised the quality and reliability of the Woodinville employees’ work. “I am grateful to every one of them,” he said, “and especially to those who chose to stay with us through two and a half years of uncertainty and kept doing their jobs with integrity.”
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler

articles.title: Power outage takes down KEXP streaming for Seattle radio station’s worldwide audience
articles.content: Seattle independent radio station KEXP, based in Lower Queen Anne, lost power early Friday morning. (GeekWire Photo / Kurt Schlosser) KEXP’s website and online streaming were down Friday morning after a power outage hit the Seattle radio station, though its over-the-air broadcast was back and running. The outage started around midnight, and the station was on and off for a while before it was “knocked offline by a major power outage” between 2 and 3 a.m., said Dashel Schueler, KEXP’s director of marketing and communications. Schueler didn’t know the cause of the outage. The station’s backup power system, known as an uninterruptible power supply (UPS), also failed. “There’s no power to the server room infrastructure because the UPS that is supposed to protect all of that gear has failed,” Schueler said. Staff are trying to power critical devices to restore services while they wait for the UPS to be repaired or for a workaround that bypasses it. There’s no estimate yet for when streaming will return. Related Seattle’s KEXP eyes a second physical home — in San Francisco’s historic Haight-Ashbury Listeners in the Seattle area can tune in at 90.3 FM. The outage affects the KEXP.org stream and the station’s mobile app. KEXP estimates about 175,000 people stream its live broadcast each week, and another 85,000 listen to its shows on-demand. The outage also took down 92.7 KREV, the station KEXP now owns in the San Francisco Bay Area, which relies on KEXP’s Seattle-based digital infrastructure. Because KEXP’s DJs pick songs live rather than playing a preset playlist, underwriting breaks vary in timing and length, Schueler said. DJs fire the separate Seattle and Bay Area spots manually and at the same time. KREV was back by around 8:30 to 8:45 a.m., running on a barebones setup KEXP typically uses for remote broadcasts, Schueler said. Listeners may notice some issues while the station gets everything put back together. Around 7:30 a.m., KEXP DJ John Richards read messages on air from listeners across Seattle who were happy to have the station back — terrestrially at least. A few posts from listeners on X and Bluesky referenced the streaming outage.
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser

articles.title: Samsung Mocks iPhone Duo Display Cracks in New Ad Campaign
articles.content: Samsung this week launched an advertising campaign mocking the display issues some people have had with the iPhone Duo . In an Instagram post on its Canadian account, Samsung shared several images showing a bright line through the spot where ‌iPhone Duo‌ models have been experiencing display problems. There are three images, each with different text: Folding is nothing new to us Folding. We know a thing or eight. Switch to Galaxy Z Fold8 A Samsung spokesperson said it's a "playful new campaign" that taps into the conversation about the "growing rivalry in foldables and how experience plays in the category." The first Galaxy foldable smartphone came out in September 2019, and the company introduced its eighth-generation Galaxy Z Fold8 three months ahead of when the ‌iPhone Duo‌ debuted. Shortly after the ‌iPhone Duo‌ launched, some customers ran into hinge issues that caused cracks in the inner display . Affected devices seem to break in the same spot, with a bright line appearing on the OLED screen. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Samsung Canada (@samsungcanada) Apple said it is aware of the issue and that only a small number of ‌iPhone Duo‌ units have a problem. Customers who have a faulty device will see the issue early on, and users with a broken ‌iPhone Duo‌ should contact Apple for a replacement. The response to iPhone Duo from early users has been incredibly positive, and we are seeing exciting things from developers who are rapidly updating their apps to take advantage of its unique form factor. We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units. If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement. The ‌iPhone Duo‌ is backordered until January for online orders, though Apple has had some in-store stock available sporadically. There do not appear to be supply issues for the Galaxy Z Fold8, with many colors and capacities delivering on November 3. Apple's ‌iPhone Duo‌ is priced starting at $1,999 for 256GB of storage, while Samsung is charging $1,899 for the same capacity.
